faqs.question: Does Move file keep the document's metadata and versions?
faqs.answer: Version history moves with the file. Metadata is kept for columns that exist in both libraries with matching internal names.

faqs.question: How do I stop a flow running before the user has filled in the properties?
faqs.answer: Add a trigger condition that requires the metadata columns to be filled, so the flow starts on the modification that completes them.

create-a-metadata-synchronization-flow.shortDescription: Keep copied values in step between SharePoint lists: when a parent item changes, a flow updates the related child items, without loops or needless runs.
create-a-metadata-synchronization-flow.fullDescription: Child items often carry copies of parent values such as project name, status or owner so that views and filters work. Copies go stale unless something updates them. This flow fires only when the watched columns change, finds the children with a delegable filter, updates only rows that differ and avoids triggering itself.
create-a-metadata-synchronization-flow.problemStatement: A project is renamed or its owner changes, and hundreds of related tasks and documents still show the old value.
whenToUse: Parent and child lists where children store copies of parent fields
Document libraries that carry project or customer metadata
When lookups alone cannot provide the filtering or grouping needed
whenNotToUse: A lookup column with additional fields already shows the parent value live
Dataverse tables, where relationships, rollups or column mappings are the better tools
create-a-metadata-synchronization-flow.formulaOrCode:
Parent list: Projects      ID | Title | ProjectStatus (choice) | ProjectOwner (person) | SyncVersion (number)
Child list:  Project Tasks  ProjectId (number, indexed) | ProjectTitle | ProjectStatus (text) | ProjectOwnerEmail (text)

Trigger: SharePoint - When an item is created or modified (Projects)
  The trigger fires for every edit. Find out whether the watched columns changed:

1. Get changes for an item or a file (properties only)
     ID: trigger ID       Since: Trigger Window Start Token       Until: Trigger Window End Token
   Outputs "Has Column Changed: Title", "Has Column Changed: ProjectStatus", "Has Column Changed: ProjectOwner"
   (requires version history on the list)

2. Condition: any watched column changed
     @or(equals(body('Get_changes')?['ColumnHasChanged']?['Title'], true),
         equals(body('Get_changes')?['ColumnHasChanged']?['ProjectStatus'], true),
         equals(body('Get_changes')?['ColumnHasChanged']?['ProjectOwner'], true))
   No > Terminate (Succeeded)

3. Get items (Project Tasks)
     Filter Query: ProjectId eq @{triggerOutputs()?['body/ID']}
     Top Count: 5000        Settings > Pagination: On, threshold 20000
     Limit columns by view to keep the payload small

4. Filter array: only children that differ (saves actions and avoids pointless versions)
     @or(not(equals(item()?['ProjectTitle'], triggerOutputs()?['body/Title'])),
         not(equals(item()?['ProjectStatus'], triggerOutputs()?['body/ProjectStatus/Value'])),
         not(equals(toLower(coalesce(item()?['ProjectOwnerEmail'], '')),
                    toLower(coalesce(triggerOutputs()?['body/ProjectOwner/Email'], '')))))

5. Apply to each (body of Filter array)      Settings > Concurrency: On, degree 10
     Send an HTTP request to SharePoint      updates without creating a new version or changing Modified By
       Method: POST
       Uri: _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Project Tasks')/items(@{items('Apply_to_each')?['ID']})/ValidateUpdateListItem
       Body:
       {
         "formValues": [
           { "FieldName": "ProjectTitle",      "FieldValue": "@{triggerOutputs()?['body/Title']}" },
           { "FieldName": "ProjectStatus",     "FieldValue": "@{triggerOutputs()?['body/ProjectStatus/Value']}" },
           { "FieldName": "ProjectOwnerEmail", "FieldValue": "@{triggerOutputs()?['body/ProjectOwner/Email']}" }
         ],
         "bNewDocumentUpdate": true
       }
     "bNewDocumentUpdate": true makes it a system-style update: no new version, Modified unchanged.
     Use the ordinary Update item action if a version and audit entry are wanted.

6. Compose summary: length(body('Filter_array')) rows updated. Log it to a flow run log list if runs are audited.

Avoiding loops
  This flow updates the child list, not the list that triggers it, so it cannot retrigger itself.
  If a second flow listens on Project Tasks, give it a trigger condition that ignores the service account:
    @not(equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/Editor/Email'], 'svc-flow@contoso.com'))
  or rely on the system-style update above, which still fires triggers but can be filtered by unchanged columns.

Trigger condition to cut runs further (optional, when only status matters)
  Keep a hidden text column LastSyncedStatus on the parent, and use:
    @not(equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/ProjectStatus/Value'], triggerOutputs()?['body/LastSyncedStatus']))
  The flow's last step writes LastSyncedStatus, which fires the trigger once more and is then stopped by the condition.

Large numbers of children (thousands)
  Batch updates through the SharePoint $batch endpoint, 100 changes per request, or run the update in a child
  flow per 1,000 items. Expect about 600 SharePoint connector calls per minute per connection.

Reconciliation (Recurrence, weekly)
  For each active project, repeat steps 3 to 5. It repairs anything missed while the flow was off or failed.

Document libraries
  Same pattern with Get files (properties only) and a ProjectId column on the library. Checked-out files cannot
  be updated: collect their names and report them.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide which parent columns are copied to children and add matching child columns.
Index the child column that stores the parent ID.
Trigger on parent changes and use Get changes to detect the watched columns.
Get the children with a filter query and pagination.
Filter to the rows that actually differ.
Update them with concurrency and a system-style update if no version is wanted.
Add a weekly reconciliation run.
commonMistakes: Updating every child on every parent edit.
Filtering children on a lookup column's text, which is slow or not delegable.
Triggering on the same list the flow updates, creating a loop.
Leaving pagination off and syncing only the first 100 children.
troubleshooting: If Get changes returns nothing, version history is off on the list or the since token is missing.
If only 100 children update, turn on pagination and set Top Count.
If updates fail with 429, lower the concurrency and let the default retry policy run.
If person values do not match, compare emails in lower case and store the email as text on the child.

faqs.question: How do I update child items when a parent item changes in SharePoint?
faqs.answer: Trigger a flow on the parent list, check that the relevant columns changed, get the children with a filter on the parent ID and update each one.

faqs.question: How do I know which column changed in a SharePoint trigger?
faqs.answer: Use the Get changes for an item or a file action with the trigger window tokens. It returns a true or false value for each column.

faqs.question: How do I update a SharePoint item without creating a new version?
faqs.answer: Call ValidateUpdateListItem through Send an HTTP request to SharePoint with bNewDocumentUpdate set to true.

create-a-flow-ownership-transfer-checkli.shortDescription: A checklist for moving a Power Automate flow from one owner to another: connections, connection references, licences, shared resources and a tested first run.
create-a-flow-ownership-transfer-checkli.fullDescription: A flow runs with its owner's connections. When that person changes role or leaves, the flow keeps running until a password changes or the account is disabled, then fails. Transferring ownership properly means adding the new owner, replacing every connection, checking licences and proving the flow still works, ideally before the old account goes.
create-a-flow-ownership-transfer-checkli.problemStatement: Someone leaves, their account is disabled, and a week later a critical flow has been failing silently because every connection was theirs.
whenToUse: An owner is leaving, changing role or handing over a solution
Moving a personal flow to a service account or a team
During joiner, mover and leaver processing
whenNotToUse: Flows that are no longer needed, which should be turned off and deleted instead
Moving a flow between environments, which is a solution export and import, not an ownership transfer
create-a-flow-ownership-transfer-checkli.formulaOrCode:
Before the transfer
  [ ] Flow name, environment, solution (or "not in a solution"), business owner, criticality
  [ ] New owner named. Prefer a service account or a team (security group) plus two named co-owners.
  [ ] New owner has the licence the flow needs:
        Standard connectors only        > Microsoft 365 licence
        Premium or custom connectors    > Power Automate Premium for the owner, or a Process licence on the flow
  [ ] New owner has access to everything the flow touches:
        SharePoint sites and lists, mailboxes (Send As / shared mailbox), Teams channels, Dataverse security roles,
        SQL or on-premises gateway (must be a gateway user), third-party accounts and API keys
  [ ] List every connection and who owns it: flow details page > Connections; in a solution > Connection references

Transfer: flow inside a solution
  [ ] Environment admin opens the solution > flow > Details > Edit > Primary owner > set the new owner
      PowerShell alternative:
        Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole -EnvironmentName <env id> -FlowName <flow id> -PrincipalType User
                               -PrincipalObjectId <new owner object id> -RoleName CanEdit
      Changing the primary owner of a solution flow:  update the workflow row's ownerid (Dataverse) or use the
      "Change owner" option in the flow's details panel.
  [ ] New owner signs in, opens each connection reference and selects or creates THEIR connection
  [ ] Turn the flow off and on once so the trigger re-registers with the new connection

Transfer: flow not in a solution
  [ ] Current owner (or an admin through the admin centre: Environments > Resources > Flows > Manage sharing)
      adds the new owner as a co-owner
  [ ] New owner opens the flow, edits each action's connection (the "..." menu or the Connections panel) and
      switches it to their own; save
  [ ] The original owner cannot be removed from a non-solution flow by themselves. Options:
        add the flow to a solution, then change the primary owner; or
        Save As / export and import a copy under the new owner, turn the old one off, and delete it after a
        parallel run
  [ ] Check "Run-only users" for instant flows: connections may be set to "Provided by run-only user" or to a
      specific connection that must be replaced

Things that carry the old owner's identity
  [ ] Approvals: requests are sent from the connection's user. Check wording and that in-flight approvals finish
      before switching.
  [ ] Emails "sent from" the owner's mailbox: switch to a shared mailbox (Send an email from a shared mailbox V2)
  [ ] SharePoint "Modified By" and Teams "posted by" will now show the new account
  [ ] Triggers on personal resources (My OneDrive, my mailbox, my calendar, Forms the person owns):
        move the form to a group (Forms > Move to a group), move files to a SharePoint library, use a shared mailbox
  [ ] Child flows: connections must be embedded ("Use this connection"), not run-only user
  [ ] Custom connectors and gateways shared with the new owner
  [ ] Environment variables and secrets (Key Vault access for the new identity)
  [ ] Power Apps that call the flow: open the app, refresh the flow, republish if the connection set changed

Test
  [ ] Trigger a real or test run. Every action succeeds with the new connections.
  [ ] Run history shows no action still using the previous owner's connection
        (flow details > Connections lists only the new owner's)
  [ ] Disable nothing on the old account until this passes

Clean up
  [ ] Remove the previous owner as co-owner (if not the unremovable creator)
  [ ] Delete the previous owner's unused connections
  [ ] Update the flow inventory and support guide: owner, co-owners, service account, date transferred
  [ ] Add a calendar check a week later: 28-day run history shows no failures

When the owner has already left
  [ ] Admin: Power Platform admin centre > Environments > Resources > Flows > select the flow > Manage sharing >
      add an owner. Or Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole.
  [ ] Flows of deleted users are listed as orphaned; the CoE Starter Kit and Get-AdminFlow help find them
  [ ] Then follow the connection and test steps above. Connections of a disabled account cannot be repaired;
      they must be replaced.
stepByStepInstructions: Record the flow, its connections and what each connects to.
Confirm the new owner's licence and access to every resource.
Add the new owner, or change the primary owner for solution flows.
Replace every connection or connection reference with the new owner's.
Move personal triggers and mailboxes to shared resources.
Run the flow and confirm no action uses the previous owner's connection.
Remove old access and update the inventory.
commonMistakes: Adding a co-owner and assuming the connections changed too.
Transferring to a person without the required premium licence.
Leaving triggers on a personal OneDrive, mailbox or form.
Disabling the leaver's account before the transfer is tested.
troubleshooting: If the flow fails with an unauthorized error after transfer, one action still uses the previous owner's connection.
If the trigger stops firing, turn the flow off and on so the trigger subscription is recreated.
If the new owner cannot select a connection reference, they need access to the solution and their own connection in that environment.
If the flow is suspended for licensing, assign Power Automate Premium to the new owner or a Process licence to the flow.

faqs.question: How do I change the owner of a Power Automate flow?
faqs.answer: For a solution flow, change the primary owner in the flow's details. For other flows, add the new person as a co-owner and replace the connections, or move the flow into a solution first.

faqs.question: What happens to flows when the owner leaves the company?
faqs.answer: They keep running until the owner's connections stop working, then fail. An admin can add a new owner, who must replace every connection.

faqs.question: Does adding a co-owner change the flow's connections?
faqs.answer: No. The flow keeps using the original connections until each one is switched to the new owner's.

create-a-connector-dependency-register.shortDescription: A register of which connectors, connections and accounts each flow and app depends on, built from the admin PowerShell cmdlets, so the impact of a change is known in advance.
create-a-connector-dependency-register.fullDescription: A DLP policy change, a retiring connector, an expiring service account password or a licence review all raise the same question: which flows and apps are affected? A dependency register answers it. It is generated from the platform, not typed by hand, and refreshed on a schedule.
create-a-connector-dependency-register.problemStatement: The admin team wants to block a connector or rotate an account's password and cannot say what will break.
whenToUse: Before changing DLP policies
Service account password rotation or account retirement
Licence reviews for premium connector use
Connector deprecations announced by Microsoft or a vendor
whenNotToUse: Tenants running the CoE Starter Kit, which already inventories connectors per app and flow
A single-maker environment with a handful of flows
create-a-connector-dependency-register.formulaOrCode:
Register columns (SharePoint list or Dataverse table "Connector Dependencies")
  ResourceType (Flow | App)   ResourceName   ResourceId   Environment   Owner   State (Started/Stopped)
  Connector (display name)    ConnectorId (shared_sharepointonline)   Tier (Standard | Premium | Custom)
  ConnectionOwner / Account   ConnectionStatus   ConnectionReference (logical name)   Endpoint (site, server, URL)
  LastSeen (date of the scan)

Build it: PowerShell (Power Platform admin; modules Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell)
  Add-PowerAppsAccount
  $rows = @()
  foreach ($env in Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment) {

      # Connector catalogue for tier lookup
      $tiers = @{}
      Get-AdminPowerAppConnector -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName | ForEach-Object {
          $tiers[$_.ConnectorName] = "Custom" }          # custom connectors in this environment
      # Standard and premium tiers: Get-PowerAppConnector (maker module) returns properties.tier per connector

      # Flows
      foreach ($f in Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName) {
          $detail = Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName -FlowName $f.FlowName
          foreach ($ref in $detail.Internal.properties.connectionReferences.PSObject.Properties) {
              $rows += [pscustomobject]@{
                  ResourceType = "Flow"; ResourceName = $f.DisplayName; ResourceId = $f.FlowName
                  Environment  = $env.DisplayName; Owner = $f.CreatedBy.userId; State = $f.Enabled
                  ConnectorId  = ($ref.Value.id -split "/")[-1]
                  Connector    = $ref.Value.displayName
                  ConnectionName = $ref.Value.connectionName
                  Tier = $ref.Value.tier
              }
          }
      }

      # Canvas apps
      foreach ($a in Get-AdminPowerApp -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName) {
          foreach ($c in $a.Internal.properties.connectionReferences.PSObject.Properties) {
              $rows += [pscustomobject]@{
                  ResourceType = "App"; ResourceName = $a.DisplayName; ResourceId = $a.AppName
                  Environment  = $env.DisplayName; Owner = $a.Owner.displayName; State = "n/a"
                  ConnectorId  = ($c.Value.id -split "/")[-1]
                  Connector    = $c.Value.displayName
                  ConnectionName = ""; Tier = $c.Value.apiTier
              }
          }
      }
  }
  $rows | Export-Csv .\connector-dependencies.csv -NoTypeInformation

  # Connections and the accounts behind them
  Get-AdminPowerAppConnection | Select-Object ConnectionName, ConnectorName, DisplayName,
      @{n="CreatedBy";e={$_.CreatedBy.userPrincipalName}}, @{n="Status";e={($_.Statuses | Select-Object -First 1).status}},
      EnvironmentName | Export-Csv .\connections.csv -NoTypeInformation
  # Join the two files on ConnectionName to see which account each flow action runs as.

Questions the register answers
  Which flows use the SQL Server connector?            filter ConnectorId = shared_sql
  What breaks if svc-flow's password is rotated?       filter ConnectionOwner = svc-flow@contoso.com
  Which resources use premium connectors, by owner?    Tier = Premium, group by Owner   (licence review)
  What would a DLP change block?                       ConnectorId in the connectors moving to Blocked, or flows that
                                                       mix connectors from the Business and Non-business groups
  Which connections are broken now?                    ConnectionStatus = Error

Endpoints (the part the cmdlets do not give)
  The site, server or URL inside each action lives in the flow definition:
    $detail.Internal.properties.definition  (triggers and actions > inputs > parameters > dataset / table / host)
  Parse for 'dataset' values to list SharePoint sites and SQL servers per flow, and for HTTP action 'uri' hosts.

Before a change
  1. Filter the register for the affected connector, connection or account.
  2. Notify owners with the list of their resources and the change date.
  3. For DLP: test the policy on a single environment first, or use the admin centre's impact view where offered.
  4. After the change, check ConnectionStatus and failed runs for the listed flows.

Keep it current
  Run the script weekly from Azure Automation or a scheduled task with a service principal
  (New-PowerAppManagementApp registers the app for admin cmdlets). Load the CSV into the list with a flow,
  set LastSeen, and flag rows not seen in the latest scan as removed.

In solutions
  Connection references are the unit of dependency: Solutions > Connection references shows each one and the
  flows that use it. One reference per connector and purpose keeps the register short.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the register list or table.
Run the script to export connector use for flows and apps in every environment.
Export connections with their owning accounts and join on connection name.
Add endpoints by parsing flow definitions where needed.
Load the result into the register and build views by connector, account and tier.
Use the register to assess and announce each change.
Schedule the scan weekly and track removed rows.
commonMistakes: Maintaining the register by hand, so it is wrong within a month.
Listing connectors without the account behind each connection.
Forgetting canvas apps, which have their own connections.
Scanning only the default environment.
troubleshooting: If the cmdlets return nothing for an environment, the account needs Power Platform admin rights or environment admin in each one.
If connection references are empty for a flow, request the single flow with its name to get the full definition.
If tiers are blank, read the connector's tier from Get-PowerAppConnector and join on the connector id.
If the scan is slow in large tenants, run per environment in parallel or query the Dataverse workflow and connectionreference tables for solution flows.

faqs.question: How do I find which flows use a particular connector?
faqs.answer: Run Get-AdminFlow for each environment and read the connection references in each flow's properties, then filter by connector id. The CoE Starter Kit provides the same view.

faqs.question: How do I know what a DLP policy change will break?
faqs.answer: Compare the connectors each flow and app uses with the policy's groups. Any resource using a blocked connector, or mixing business and non-business connectors, will be suspended.

faqs.question: How do I see which account a flow's connections use?
faqs.answer: Export connections with Get-AdminPowerAppConnection, which shows who created each one, and join that to the flow's connection names.

create-a-failed-run-triage-process.shortDescription: A triage process for failed Power Automate runs: collect failures in one place, classify the error, apply the standard fix, resubmit, and record the cause.
create-a-failed-run-triage-process.fullDescription: Flows fail for a small number of reasons: a connection expired, a service throttled, the data was not what the flow expected, or a permission changed. A triage process brings failures to one list, sorts them by cause using the error code, gives each cause a standard response and makes sure failed work is resubmitted instead of lost.
create-a-failed-run-triage-process.problemStatement: Failure emails go to one maker's inbox and are ignored. Nobody knows which runs failed, whether the work was redone, or why it keeps happening.
whenToUse: Any environment with business-critical flows
Support teams taking over flows from makers
When the same failures recur
whenNotToUse: Personal productivity flows, where the weekly failure email to the owner is enough
Environments already monitored through Application Insights alerts with an on-call process
create-a-failed-run-triage-process.formulaOrCode:
1. Capture
  In every important flow: Scope "Try" + Scope "Catch" (run after: has failed, has timed out).
  Catch writes one row to a shared "Flow Failures" list, then Terminate (Failed):
    FlowName       workflow()?['tags']?['flowDisplayName']
    RunLink        concat('https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/', workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName'],
                          '/flows/', workflow()?['name'], '/runs/', workflow()?['run']?['name'])
    FailedAction   first(body('Filter_failed'))?['name']
    ErrorCode      coalesce(first(body('Filter_failed'))?['code'], first(body('Filter_failed'))?['outputs']?['statusCode'])
    ErrorMessage   coalesce(first(body('Filter_failed'))?['error']?['message'],
                            first(body('Filter_failed'))?['outputs']?['body']?['message'])
    RecordKey      the business identifier (item ID, order number) so the work can be found
    where Filter_failed = Filter array on result('Try') with  @equals(item()?['status'], 'Failed')
  List columns to add: Category (choice), Status (New | Investigating | Resubmitted | Fixed | Ignored),
    AssignedTo, RootCause, FixApplied, ClosedOn
  Flows without a catch scope: admins can list failures with PowerShell
    Get-FlowRun -EnvironmentName <env> -FlowName <flow id> | Where-Object Status -eq "Failed"
  or route cloud flow telemetry to Application Insights (environment setting > Data export).

2. Classify by error
  Code / text                                  Category          Usual cause
  401, 403 "Unauthorized", "connection is     Connection        password changed, token expired, account
    not configured", InvalidConnection                           disabled, permission removed
  429, "Rate limit", "TooManyRequests"        Throttling        loop without delay, bulk load, shared limits
  408, 502, 503, 504, "GatewayTimeout"        Transient         service or network blip
  400 "BadRequest", "InvalidTemplate",        Data or logic     null value, wrong type, missing column,
    "The template language expression..."                        bad expression, required field empty
  404 "NotFound"                               Missing resource  item, file, list or site deleted or renamed
  409, 412 "Conflict", "Precondition failed"   Concurrency       two runs edited the same item; file locked
  "ActionTimedOut", approval timeout           Timeout           approval not answered in 30 days; long HTTP call
  "FlowSuspended", licence messages            Licence or DLP    owner licence removed; DLP policy change

3. Standard response per category
  Connection        Fix the connection as its owner (Connections > Fix connection). Resubmit failed runs.
  Throttling        Usually recovers with the built-in retry. If not: lower concurrency, add a delay, batch. Resubmit.
  Transient         Resubmit. If it recurs more than weekly, raise the action's retry policy (exponential, 4 to 6 tries).
  Data or logic     Do not resubmit unchanged: it fails again. Fix the data or the flow, then resubmit.
  Missing resource  Restore or repoint. Check whether a site, list or column was renamed.
  Concurrency       Resubmit. Add concurrency control on the trigger or check ETag before update.
  Timeout           Decide the business outcome (escalate, cancel), then rerun from a suitable point.
  Licence or DLP    Platform admin. Flow stays off until resolved.

4. Resubmit
  Run history > open the failed run > Resubmit. It reruns with the original trigger data, using the current
  version of the flow. Runs are kept for 28 days: after that the trigger data is gone.
  Many runs: Run history > select failed runs > Resubmit (bulk, up to 20 at a time in the portal), or script it:
    POST https://api.flow.microsoft.com/providers/Microsoft.ProcessSimple/environments/<env>/flows/<flow>/
         triggers/<trigger>/histories/<run>/resubmit?api-version=2016-11-01
  Before resubmitting, check the flow is safe to run twice for that record (will it send a second email,
  create a duplicate item?). Idempotent flows check for existing output first.

5. Daily routine (15 minutes)
  Open "Flow Failures" view: Status = New, grouped by FlowName.
  Set Category from the error. Apply the standard response. Set Status and FixApplied.
  Same flow and category three times in a week > raise a problem record for a permanent fix.

6. Weekly review
  Failures by flow and by category (group and count in the list, or a Power BI report).
  Top three recurring causes get an owner and a due date.
  Flows with no failures recorded but known to be critical: confirm their catch scope works by forcing a test failure.

7. Alerts
  Flow on "Flow Failures" item created: post to the support Teams channel for flows marked critical.
  Avoid alert floods: one message per flow per hour (check for an existing New item for the same flow in the last hour).
stepByStepInstructions: Add try and catch scopes to important flows and log failures to one list.
Add category, status and root cause columns to the list.
Classify each new failure from its error code.
Apply the standard response for that category.
Resubmit runs once the cause is fixed, checking for duplicate side effects.
Review counts weekly and assign permanent fixes for repeat causes.
Alert the support channel for critical flows without flooding it.
commonMistakes: Resubmitting data or logic failures without changing anything.
Leaving failures to the default email that only the owner sees.
Waiting more than 28 days, after which runs cannot be resubmitted.
Resubmitting flows that send emails or create items without checking for duplicates.
troubleshooting: If the catch scope never runs, set its run after to has failed and has timed out, not is successful.
If the error message is blank, read outputs.body.message or outputs.body.error.message for connector actions.
If Resubmit is greyed out, the run is older than 28 days or the trigger type does not support it.
If the failure list fills with one error, fix that cause first and add the hourly limit to alerts.

faqs.question: How do I find all failed flow runs?
faqs.answer: Log failures from a catch scope to a shared list, use the flow's 28-day run history filtered to failed, or list them with Get-FlowRun in PowerShell.

faqs.question: How do I rerun a failed Power Automate flow?
faqs.answer: Open the failed run in run history and select Resubmit. It runs again with the original trigger data and the current flow definition.

faqs.question: What causes most Power Automate failures?
faqs.answer: Expired or broken connections, throttling, transient service errors and unexpected data such as null values or missing columns.

create-a-notification-throttling-pattern.shortDescription: Stop a flow flooding people with messages: send at most one notification per subject per period, collect the rest, and deliver them as a single digest.
create-a-notification-throttling-pattern.fullDescription: A flow that emails on every change is fine at five items a day and unbearable at five hundred. Throttling keeps a small log of what was sent to whom and when. Before sending, the flow checks the log: if a recent message exists for the same key it queues the event instead, and a scheduled flow sends the queue as one summary.
create-a-notification-throttling-pattern.problemStatement: A bulk edit or a busy day triggers hundreds of near-identical emails or Teams posts. People create inbox rules to hide them and then miss the one that mattered.
whenToUse: Notifications triggered by item changes, failures or thresholds
Alerts to shared mailboxes and Teams channels
Flows that can be triggered in bulk by imports or other flows
whenNotToUse: Messages that must be delivered individually for audit or legal reasons
Low-volume flows where every event deserves its own message
create-a-notification-throttling-pattern.formulaOrCode:
List: Notification Log
  Title (NotificationKey, indexed)   Recipient (text, indexed)   LastSentOn (date and time)   PendingCount (number)
  PendingDetails (multiple lines, plain text)   Window (number of minutes, optional override)

NotificationKey: what counts as "the same" notification
  per item and recipient:        concat('Request-', ID, '-', recipientEmail)
  per flow failure:              concat('FlowFailure-', flowName)
  per recipient and category:    concat('Overdue-', ownerEmail)

In the notifying flow (after the event is detected)
  1. Compose Key:      concat('Request-', triggerOutputs()?['body/ID'], '-', variables('recipient'))
  2. Compose Line:     concat(formatDateTime(utcNow(), 'HH:mm'), ' ', triggerOutputs()?['body/Title'], ' changed to ',
                              triggerOutputs()?['body/Status/Value'])
  3. Get items (Notification Log)   Filter Query: Title eq '@{outputs('Key')}'    Top Count: 1
  4. Compose WindowStart:  addMinutes(utcNow(), -60)          60-minute quiet period
  5. Condition: send now?
       @or(empty(body('Get_items')?['value']),
           less(first(body('Get_items')?['value'])?['LastSentOn'], outputs('WindowStart')))
     Yes:
       Send the email or Teams message
       If no log row: Create item  Title = Key, Recipient, LastSentOn = utcNow(), PendingCount = 0
       Else:          Update item  LastSentOn = utcNow(), PendingCount = 0, PendingDetails = ''
     No (within the quiet period): queue it
       Update item  PendingCount = add(first(...)?['PendingCount'], 1)
                    PendingDetails = concat(first(...)?['PendingDetails'], outputs('Line'), decodeUriComponent('%0A'))

  Race condition: two runs can both find no row and both send. Reduce it with trigger concurrency = 1 for
  low-volume flows, or accept an occasional double send. For strict once-only, create the log row first with
  "enforce unique values" on Title and treat a failed create as "someone else is sending".

Digest flow (Recurrence, every 60 minutes, or 08:00 and 13:00 for a calmer rhythm)
  1. Get items (Notification Log)   Filter Query: PendingCount gt 0
  2. Apply to each:
       Send one message:  "<PendingCount> further updates since <LastSentOn>" followed by PendingDetails
       Update item: LastSentOn = utcNow(), PendingCount = 0, PendingDetails = ''
  Group by Recipient first (Select + union for distinct recipients) to send one message per person, not per key.

Simpler variants
  A. Trigger-side throttling when only the latest state matters
     Trigger condition so the flow runs only for the change that matters:
       @equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/Status/Value'], 'Approved')
     plus a "NotifiedOn" column on the item; skip if NotifiedOn is within the last hour.
  B. Debounce: wait for edits to stop
     Delay 5 minutes > Get item > continue only if Modified equals the trigger's Modified.
     Earlier runs end quietly; the last edit sends the message. Costs a waiting run per edit.
  C. Digest only
     Never send from the trigger flow. A scheduled flow queries what changed since its last run
     (Modified ge '@{addHours(utcNow(), -24)}') and sends one summary per owner.

Teams specifics
  Post one parent message per key and add replies for later events ("Reply with a message in a channel"),
  storing the parent's messageId in the log. The channel shows one thread instead of fifty posts.
  Chat and channel posting is throttled by Teams (about one message per second per flow connection):
  keep concurrency low when posting in loops.

Email specifics
  Outlook connector: about 300 API calls per 60 seconds per connection, and Exchange limits of 10,000 recipients
  per day and 30 messages per minute for a mailbox. A digest stays far below these.

Give people control
  Preferences list: Recipient | Category | Mode (Immediate | Hourly digest | Daily digest | Off)
  Look it up before step 5 and choose the window or skip.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide the key that defines a duplicate notification and the quiet period.
Create the notification log list with an indexed key.
In the notifying flow, look up the key before sending.
Send and stamp the log when outside the quiet period, otherwise add the event to the pending details.
Build the scheduled digest flow that sends and clears pending entries.
For Teams, reply in one thread per key.
Add a preferences list if recipients want different rhythms.
commonMistakes: Throttling by dropping events, so information is lost instead of summarised.
A key that is too broad, which hides unrelated alerts behind one message.
No digest flow, leaving queued events unsent.
High concurrency that lets many runs pass the check at once.
troubleshooting: If duplicates still arrive in bursts, runs are checking the log at the same moment. Lower trigger concurrency or use the unique-key create approach.
If the digest is empty, PendingCount is not being incremented. Check the false branch updates the row found in Get items.
If PendingDetails is cut off, the plain text column limit was reached. Cap the lines stored and show the count.
If Teams posts fail with 429, add a one-second delay inside the loop.

faqs.question: How do I stop Power Automate sending too many emails?
faqs.answer: Record when each notification was last sent, skip or queue further ones inside a quiet period, and send the queued events as one digest on a schedule.

faqs.question: How do I send one summary email instead of many?
faqs.answer: Use a scheduled flow that gathers the pending events or recently changed items, groups them by recipient and sends each person a single message.

faqs.question: How do I wait until a user has finished editing before notifying?
faqs.answer: Add a short delay, re-read the item and continue only if its modified time still matches the trigger. Only the last edit gets through.

create-a-reusable-approval-child-flow.shortDescription: One child flow that runs approvals for every process: the parent passes title, approvers and a link, and gets back the outcome, approver and comments in a standard shape.
create-a-reusable-approval-child-flow.fullDescription: Approval steps are rebuilt in flow after flow, each with slightly different reminders, timeouts and wording. A child flow in a solution holds that logic once. Parents call it with a few inputs and act on a consistent response, so a change to reminders or logging is made in one place.
create-a-reusable-approval-child-flow.problemStatement: Ten flows each contain their own approval, reminder loop and timeout handling. They behave differently and fixing a bug means editing all ten.
whenToUse: Several processes need approvals with the same behaviour
A standard approval record is required across processes
Reminders, timeouts and delegation should be consistent
whenNotToUse: A single simple flow with one approval and no reminders
Parents that are not in a solution, since child flows can only be called from solution flows
create-a-reusable-approval-child-flow.formulaOrCode:
Child flow: "Shared - Run approval"   (inside a solution)

Trigger: Manually trigger a flow     inputs:
  Title            Text      "Purchase request PR-1042: laptop"
  Details          Text      Markdown shown in the approval
  ApproverEmails   Text      semicolon-separated
  ApprovalType     Text      "First" (first to respond) or "All" (everyone must approve)
  ItemLink         Text      URL to the record
  RequestorEmail   Text
  TimeoutDays      Number    days before the approval is treated as timed out
  ProcessName      Text      for logging
  RecordKey        Text      for logging

Scope: Try
  1. Start and wait for an approval
       Approval type:  if(equals(triggerBody()?['text_3'], 'All'), 'Approve/Reject - Everyone must approve',
                          'Approve/Reject - First to respond')
                       (the action's type cannot be an expression in the designer: use a Condition with two
                        approval actions, one per type, and join the results below)
       Title, Assigned to, Details, Item link, Requestor from the inputs
       Settings > Timeout:  concat('P', string(triggerBody()?['number']), 'D')      for example P7D
  2. Parallel branch for reminders (optional)
       Do until the approval branch sets varDone = true:
         Delay TimeoutDays / 2 days > if not done, send a reminder email with the approval link
       Simpler: one Delay then one reminder, in a branch that is cancelled when the flow ends.

Scope: Timed out   (run after Try: has timed out)
  Set varOutcome = "TimedOut"

Scope: Failed      (run after Try: has failed)
  Set varOutcome = "Error"; varComments = the error message

After Try succeeds
  varOutcome   = outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/outcome']          "Approve" or "Reject"
  varApprover  = first(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses'])?['responder']?['email']
  varComments  = join(xpath(xml(json(concat('{"r":{"c":',
                   string(outputs('Start_and_wait_for_an_approval')?['body/responses']), '}}'))),
                   '/r/c/comments/text()'), ' | ')
                 or simply first(...responses)?['comments'] for first-to-respond approvals

Log (one place for every process)
  Create item in "Approval Log": ProcessName, RecordKey, Title, Outcome, Approver, Comments, RequestedOn, CompletedOn

Respond to a PowerApp or flow     (must run on every path: set run after to succeeded, failed, skipped, timed out)
  Outcome      Text     Approve | Reject | TimedOut | Error
  Approver     Text
  Comments     Text
  CompletedOn  Text     utcNow()

Child flow settings
  Run only users: set every connection to "Use this connection (<service account>)". A child flow cannot use
  "Provided by run-only user" connections.
  Connections through connection references so the solution deploys cleanly.

Parent flow
  Run a Child Flow > "Shared - Run approval"
    Title:           concat('Purchase request ', triggerOutputs()?['body/Title'])
    Details:         concat('**Amount:** ', triggerOutputs()?['body/Amount'], decodeUriComponent('%0A'),
                            '**Requested by:** ', triggerOutputs()?['body/Author/DisplayName'])
    ApproverEmails:  the manager's email, or several joined with ';'
    ApprovalType:    First
    ItemLink:        triggerOutputs()?['body/{Link}']
    TimeoutDays:     7
    ProcessName:     Purchasing        RecordKey: string(triggerOutputs()?['body/ID'])
  Switch on body('Run_a_Child_Flow')?['outcome']
    Approve   > update status to Approved, notify requester
    Reject    > update status to Rejected with comments
    TimedOut  > escalate: call the child flow again with the approver's manager, or mark "Escalated"
    Error     > notify support

Limits to design around
  A parent waits for the child's response. Flow runs last at most 30 days, so TimeoutDays plus any
  escalation round must stay under that. For longer waits, have the child update the record and end,
  and let a second flow pick up the status change.
  The synchronous Respond action must be reached within the parent's action timeout; raise the Run a Child
  Flow action's timeout setting (for example P14D) to cover the approval period.

Versioning
  Add new inputs as optional with defaults inside the child (coalesce(triggerBody()?['text_9'], 'default')).
  Removing or renaming an input breaks every parent until each is opened and saved.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the child flow in a solution with the manual trigger inputs.
Add the approval with a timeout and separate handling for timed out and failed.
Normalise outcome, approver and comments into variables.
Log the result to a shared approval log.
Add the Respond action and make it run on every path.
Set the child flow's run-only connections to fixed connections.
Call it from each parent and branch on the returned outcome.
commonMistakes: Leaving the Respond action on the success path only, so parents hang on a timeout.
Run-only user connections in the child, which block it from being called.
Timeouts longer than the 30-day run limit.
Renaming inputs after parents are live.
troubleshooting: If the child flow is not listed in Run a Child Flow, both flows must be in a solution in the same environment.
If the parent fails with a timeout while the approval is still pending, raise the timeout on the Run a Child Flow action.
If saving the parent reports the child must use embedded connections, edit the child's run-only users and choose Use this connection for each.
If comments are blank for everyone-must-approve, loop the responses array and join each responder's comments.

faqs.question: Can I reuse an approval across several flows?
faqs.answer: Yes. Put the approval in a child flow inside a solution, pass in the title, approvers and link, and return the outcome with a Respond action.

faqs.question: Why can't I select my child flow?
faqs.answer: Child flows must be in a solution, use the manual trigger, end with a Respond action and use fixed connections, not run-only user connections.

faqs.question: How long can an approval wait in a child flow?
faqs.answer: A run can last up to 30 days. Set the approval's timeout below that and handle the timed-out path, for example by escalating.

create-a-scheduled-maintenance-flow.shortDescription: A scheduled flow that does the housekeeping a solution needs: trims logs, closes abandoned drafts, checks reference data and reports what it did.
create-a-scheduled-maintenance-flow.fullDescription: Solutions accumulate debris: run logs grow past the list view threshold, drafts are abandoned, lookups point at inactive values. A weekly maintenance flow handles these in one place, in batches that respect connector limits, and sends a short report so someone knows it ran and what it changed.
create-a-scheduled-maintenance-flow.problemStatement: The log list reaches 100,000 rows and views stop working. Hundreds of draft requests from two years ago clutter every report. Nobody owns the tidying.
whenToUse: Solutions with logging, audit or staging lists
Processes that leave drafts or temporary items
As part of handing a solution to operations
whenNotToUse: Deleting business records subject to retention rules, which belongs to Purview retention
Dataverse log tables, where bulk delete jobs are the built-in tool
create-a-scheduled-maintenance-flow.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: Recurrence     Frequency: Week   On: Sunday   At: 02:00   Time zone: set explicitly
  Settings come from a "Maintenance Settings" list or environment variables, not hard-coded:
    LogRetentionDays 90      DraftAbandonDays 60      BatchSize 500      ReportTo ops@contoso.com      DryRun No

Initialize variables: varReport (array), varDeleted (integer), varClosed (integer)

Task 1: trim the run log
  Do until (no more rows or 10 loops):
    Get items (Flow Run Log)
      Filter Query: Created lt '@{addDays(utcNow(), mul(-1, variables('LogRetentionDays')))}'
      Top Count: @{variables('BatchSize')}        Order By: ID asc
      Limit columns by view: a view showing only ID
    Condition: length(body('Get_items')?['value']) equals 0 > set varDone = true
    Apply to each (concurrency 10): Delete item        (skipped when DryRun = Yes)
    Increment varDeleted by length(body('Get_items')?['value'])
  Do until limits: Count 10, Timeout PT1H. Ten loops of 500 remove 5,000 rows per run and stay within limits.
  Faster for large backlogs: one SharePoint $batch request per 100 deletes
    POST _api/$batch  with a changeset of DELETE _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Flow Run Log')/items(<id>), IF-MATCH: *
  Deleted items go to the site recycle bin and count toward storage for 93 days.

Task 2: close abandoned drafts
  Get items (Requests)
    Filter Query: Status eq 'Draft' and Modified lt '@{addDays(utcNow(), mul(-1, variables('DraftAbandonDays')))}'
    Top Count: 500
  Apply to each: Update item  Status = Cancelled, CancelReason = "Draft not submitted within 60 days"
                 (optional) email the author once with a link to reopen
  Increment varClosed.

Task 3: reference data checks (report only, change nothing)
  a. Open requests pointing at inactive categories
       Get items (Categories) IsActive eq 0 > Select IDs
       Get items (Requests) Status ne 'Closed' > Filter array where CategoryId is in the inactive IDs
  b. Open items assigned to people who have left
       For each distinct AssignedTo email: Get user profile (V2); a 404 means the account is gone.
       Configure run after on the following step to include "has failed", and collect the email.
  c. Lists close to limits
       Send an HTTP request to SharePoint: GET _api/web/lists/getbytitle('Requests')?$select=ItemCount
       Report any list over 80% of a working limit you set (for example 4,000 for unindexed views,
       or 100,000 for permission inheritance changes).
  Append each finding to varReport.

Task 4: connection and flow health
  List flows as admin (Power Automate Management connector: List Flows as Admin) for the solution's flows;
  report any that are Stopped or Suspended.
  For each critical flow, count failed rows in the Flow Failures list in the last 7 days.

Report (always sent, even when nothing was done)
  Subject: Maintenance report <solution> <date>: <varDeleted> log rows removed, <varClosed> drafts closed
  Body: HTML table from varReport (Create HTML table), settings used, DryRun state, run link:
    concat('https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/', workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName'],
           '/flows/', workflow()?['name'], '/runs/', workflow()?['run']?['name'])
  A missing Monday report is itself the signal that the flow is broken.

Structure
  Put each task in its own Scope. Set every later scope to run after the previous one "is successful, has
  failed, is skipped, has timed out" so one failing task does not stop the rest.
  Final step: if any scope failed (check result('Task_1') and so on), Terminate with status Failed after
  sending the report.

Safety
  DryRun setting for the first runs: count and report without deleting or updating.
  Never delete from business lists in this flow. Change status and let retention deal with removal.
  Run as the service account. Add the flow to the support guide with what it changes and when.

Dataverse equivalents
  Logs: Settings > Data management > Bulk deletion jobs, with a recurring schedule and a view as the filter.
  Flow run history stored in Dataverse (FlowRun table) has its own retention setting (default 28 days).
stepByStepInstructions: List the housekeeping the solution needs and the safe thresholds.
Store thresholds and the dry-run switch in a settings list or environment variables.
Build one scope per task, each able to run after a failure of the one before.
Trim logs in limited batches with a Do until loop.
Close abandoned drafts by status change, not deletion.
Add report-only checks for reference data, leavers and list sizes.
Send a report on every run and fail the run if any task failed.
commonMistakes: Deleting tens of thousands of rows in one run and hitting throttling or the action limits.
Deleting business records from a housekeeping flow.
Sending a report only when something went wrong, so a dead flow goes unnoticed.
Hard-coding thresholds inside filter queries.
troubleshooting: If Get items fails with a threshold error on the log list, index Created and filter on it first.
If the Do until stops early, raise its count and timeout limits or the batch size.
If deletes return 429, lower the loop concurrency and rely on the default retry.
If the flow ran but changed nothing, check the DryRun setting and the time zone of the date filter.

faqs.question: How do I delete old SharePoint list items automatically?
faqs.answer: Use a scheduled flow that gets items older than a cutoff date in batches and deletes them, limited per run to stay within connector limits.

faqs.question: How many items can a flow delete at once?
faqs.answer: Work in batches of a few hundred with a bounded loop, or use the SharePoint batch endpoint with 100 deletes per request. Several thousand per run is practical.

faqs.question: How do I know a scheduled flow is still running?
faqs.answer: Have it send a short report on every run. A missing report tells you it has stopped.

create-a-service-intake-workspace.shortDescription: A single canvas app screen where a service team takes in, triages and assigns requests: queue on the left, detail and actions on the right, new request in a side panel.
create-a-service-intake-workspace.fullDescription: A service desk works from one place all day. An intake workspace puts the incoming queue, the selected request and the common actions on one screen, so agents do not hop between a list, a form and a mailbox. The layout below uses a filtered gallery, a detail pane bound to the selection and a slide-in panel for logging a new request.
create-a-service-intake-workspace.problemStatement: Agents triage requests from a SharePoint list view, open each item in a form, then go back to the list. Assigning ten requests takes fifty clicks, and new phone requests are logged on paper first.
whenToUse: Shared service teams handling 20 to 300 open requests
Requests arriving by form, email and phone that need one queue
Desktop or tablet use by a small group of agents
whenNotToUse: Requester self-service, which needs a simpler screen with only the person's own items
Queues beyond a few thousand open items, where a model-driven app with views is a better fit
create-a-service-intake-workspace.formulaOrCode:
Data: Requests list
  Title, Details (multi-line), Category (choice), Priority (choice: Low, Normal, High),
  Status (choice: New, Assigned, Waiting, Resolved), AssignedTo (person), Requester (person), Channel (choice)

Screen layout (horizontal container, fills the screen)
  conQueue   width 38%   : filter row + galQueue
  conDetail  flexible    : header, facts, actions, notes
  conNew     overlay panel on the right, Visible: locShowNew

Filters (top of conQueue)
  tabStatus (Tab list or buttons): New | Mine | Waiting | All open
  txtSearch
  galQueue.Items
    SortByColumns(
        Filter(Requests,
            (locTab = "New"      && Status.Value = "New") ||
            (locTab = "Mine"     && AssignedTo.Email = gblUserEmail && Status.Value <> "Resolved") ||
            (locTab = "Waiting"  && Status.Value = "Waiting") ||
            (locTab = "All open" && Status.Value <> "Resolved"),
            StartsWith(Title, txtSearch.Text)
        ),
        "Created", SortOrder.Ascending)
  App.Formulas:  gblUserEmail = Lower(User().Email);
  Oldest first, so nothing sits at the bottom of the queue unseen.

Queue row (galQueue template)
  Title, requester name, age:  DateDiff(ThisItem.Created, Now(), TimeUnit.Hours) & " h"
  Priority bar Fill:  Switch(ThisItem.Priority.Value, "High", ColorValue("#D13438"), "Normal", ColorValue("#0078D4"), ColorValue("#8A8886"))
  TemplateFill: If(ThisItem.IsSelected, ColorValue("#EFF6FC"), Color.White)
  OnSelect: Set(gblRequest, ThisItem)

Detail pane (bound to gblRequest)
  Header: gblRequest.Title            Facts: requester, category, channel, created
  Empty state when nothing is selected: Visible: IsBlank(gblRequest)

Actions
  btnTake.OnSelect  (assign to me)
    IfError(
        Set(gblRequest, Patch(Requests, gblRequest, {
            AssignedTo: { Claims: "i:0#.f|membership|" & gblUserEmail, DisplayName: User().FullName, Email: gblUserEmail,
                          Department: "", JobTitle: "", Picture: "" },
            Status: { Value: "Assigned" } })),
        Notify("Could not assign: " & FirstError.Message, NotificationType.Error),
        Notify("Assigned to you", NotificationType.Success))
  btnTake.DisplayMode: If(gblRequest.Status.Value = "New", DisplayMode.Edit, DisplayMode.Disabled)

  Assign to a colleague: combo box cmbAgent (Items: Choices(Requests.AssignedTo), or a Support Agents list)
    Patch(Requests, gblRequest, { AssignedTo: cmbAgent.Selected, Status: { Value: "Assigned" } })

  Waiting / Resolve
    Set(gblRequest, Patch(Requests, gblRequest, { Status: { Value: "Waiting" } }))
    Resolve asks for a note first: btnResolve.DisplayMode: If(IsBlank(txtResolution.Text), Disabled, Edit)

  Refresh the row after each change: assigning Patch's result back to gblRequest keeps the detail pane current.

New request panel (phone or walk-up)
  btnNew.OnSelect: Set(locShowNew, true)
  Fields: requester (people combo box), title, category, priority, details
  btnSaveNew.OnSelect
    IfError(
        Patch(Requests, Defaults(Requests), { Title: txtNewTitle.Text, Details: txtNewDetails.Text,
              Category: drpNewCategory.Selected, Priority: drpNewPriority.Selected, Requester: cmbRequester.Selected,
              Channel: { Value: "Phone" }, Status: { Value: "New" } }),
        Notify(FirstError.Message, NotificationType.Error),
        Set(locShowNew, false); Reset(txtNewTitle); Reset(txtNewDetails); Notify("Request logged", NotificationType.Success))

Counts on the tabs
  "New (" & CountRows(Filter(Requests, Status.Value = "New")) & ")"
  CountRows over a SharePoint filter is not delegable. Keep open items under 2,000, or show counts from a
  collection refreshed with the queue.

Keep it current
  Timer, 60 seconds, OnTimerEnd: Refresh(Requests)   paused while a panel is open.
stepByStepInstructions: Create or confirm the Requests list with status, priority, category and assignee columns.
Lay out the screen as a queue pane and a detail pane in a horizontal container.
Bind the gallery to a delegable filter driven by status tabs and search.
Show the selected request in the detail pane with an empty state.
Add take, assign, waiting and resolve actions that patch and refresh the selected record.
Add a side panel for logging new requests and a timer to refresh the queue.
commonMistakes: Sorting newest first, which hides the oldest waiting items.
Navigating to a separate form for every action.
Tab counts that silently stop at 500 because the count is not delegable.
No empty state when nothing is selected.
troubleshooting: If the detail pane shows stale values, set the variable to the record returned by Patch.
If assignment fails, check the person record includes Claims with the membership prefix.
If the Mine tab is empty, compare lower-case emails on both sides.
If the queue misses items, look for a delegation warning on the gallery's Items.

faqs.question: What is a service intake workspace in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: One screen that combines the request queue, the selected request's details and the triage actions, so agents work without switching screens.

faqs.question: How do I assign a request to myself in a canvas app?
faqs.answer: Patch the person column with a record containing your claims, display name and email, and set the status in the same call.

faqs.question: Should the queue sort newest or oldest first?
faqs.answer: Oldest first for work queues, so the longest-waiting request is always at the top.

create-a-mobile-field-update-form.shortDescription: A phone-first form for field staff to update a job in under a minute: large controls, one column, photo and location capture, and a save that survives poor signal.
create-a-mobile-field-update-form.fullDescription: Field updates happen standing up, one-handed, often with weak coverage. A form designed for a desk fails there. This pattern keeps the screen to one column of large controls, captures a photo and GPS position with the update, queues the save when offline and confirms clearly when it has gone through.
create-a-mobile-field-update-form.problemStatement: Technicians are given the office app on their phones. Controls are tiny, the form has thirty fields, and an update typed in a basement is lost when the save fails with no signal.
whenToUse: Job, inspection or delivery updates made on site from a phone
Updates that need a photo, a reading or a location
Areas with unreliable mobile coverage
whenNotToUse: Data entry of long records, which belongs on a tablet or desktop layout
Processes needing guaranteed real-time data, where offline queuing causes conflicts
create-a-mobile-field-update-form.formulaOrCode:
App set-up
  Phone layout (640 x 1136). Settings > Display: Scale to fit On, Lock orientation On.
  One screen for the job list, one for the update. No more than seven inputs on the update screen.

Update screen (vertical container, padding 16, gap 12)
  Job header: number, address, customer (read-only)
  Status: three large buttons instead of a drop-down
    btnOnSite / btnDone / btnBlocked      Height 64
    OnSelect: UpdateContext({ locStatus: "Done" })
    Fill: If(locStatus = "Done", ColorValue("#107C10"), ColorValue("#F3F2F1"))
  Reading: txtReading   Format: TextFormat.Number   (brings up the numeric keypad)   Height 56, Size 20
  Note: txtNote   Mode: MultiLine   Height 120
  Photo: Add picture control (camera or gallery)    imgPreview.Image: AddMediaButton1.Media
  Location label: If(IsBlank(Location.Latitude), "Location unavailable", Text(Location.Latitude, "0.00000") & ", " & Text(Location.Longitude, "0.00000"))
  Save button: full width, Height 64, pinned to the bottom

Minimum sizes
  Touch targets 48 px or more, text 16 px or more, 12 px between controls. Labels above fields, never beside.

Save (works online or offline)
  btnSave.OnSelect
    UpdateContext({ locSaving: true });
    With({ upd: { JobId: gblJob.ID, Status: locStatus, Reading: Value(txtReading.Text), Note: txtNote.Text,
                  Lat: Location.Latitude, Lon: Location.Longitude, At: Now(),
                  Photo: AddMediaButton1.Media, Key: Text(GUID()) } },
        If(Connection.Connected,
            IfError(
                Patch('Job Updates', Defaults('Job Updates'),
                      { Title: gblJob.Title, JobId: upd.JobId, Status: { Value: upd.Status }, Reading: upd.Reading,
                        Note: upd.Note, Latitude: upd.Lat, Longitude: upd.Lon, CapturedAt: upd.At, ClientKey: upd.Key });
                Patch(Jobs, gblJob, { Status: { Value: upd.Status } }),
                Collect(colPending, upd); SaveData(colPending, "pendingUpdates");
                Notify("Saved on this phone. It will send when you are back online.", NotificationType.Warning),
                Notify("Update sent", NotificationType.Success)),
            Collect(colPending, upd); SaveData(colPending, "pendingUpdates");
            Notify("No signal. Saved on this phone.", NotificationType.Warning)));
    UpdateContext({ locSaving: false, locStatus: Blank() }); Reset(txtReading); Reset(txtNote); Reset(AddMediaButton1);
    Back()

Send queued updates
  App.OnStart: LoadData(colPending, "pendingUpdates", true)
  Timer (30 s) OnTimerEnd, or a "Send now" button:
    If(Connection.Connected && CountRows(colPending) > 0,
        ForAll(colPending As p,
            If(IsBlank(LookUp('Job Updates', ClientKey = p.Key)),
               Patch('Job Updates', Defaults('Job Updates'),
                     { Title: "Job " & p.JobId, JobId: p.JobId, Status: { Value: p.Status }, Reading: p.Reading,
                       Note: p.Note, Latitude: p.Lat, Longitude: p.Lon, CapturedAt: p.At, ClientKey: p.Key })));
        Clear(colPending); SaveData(colPending, "pendingUpdates"))
  ClientKey prevents a duplicate when a save succeeded but the reply was lost.
  Badge on the home screen: CountRows(colPending) & " waiting to send"

Photos
  Send the image to a flow that creates a file in a library (Power Apps V2 trigger with a file input), keyed
  by ClientKey. Reduce size first: Add picture control's image is already compressed on most phones.
  Keep photos in colPending with the update so they are sent together.

Job list for offline use
  OnStart when connected: ClearCollect(colMyJobs, Filter(Jobs, AssignedTo.Email = User().Email, Status.Value <> "Closed"));
                          SaveData(colMyJobs, "myJobs")
  When not connected: LoadData(colMyJobs, "myJobs", true)

Test on the real device, outdoors, with gloves if staff wear them, and in airplane mode.
stepByStepInstructions: Build a phone-layout app with a job list and a single-column update screen.
Use large buttons for status and number-format inputs for readings.
Capture photo, location and time with each update.
Save directly when connected and queue to a local collection when not.
Send queued updates on reconnect, using a client key to avoid duplicates.
Test in airplane mode and on the phones staff carry.
commonMistakes: Shrinking a desktop form onto a phone.
Losing the entry when a save fails.
Drop-downs for a three-option status.
No visible count of updates waiting to send.
troubleshooting: If SaveData fails in a browser, run the app in the Power Apps mobile player.
If location is blank, the user declined permission or is indoors. Allow saving without it.
If duplicates appear after reconnecting, check the client key lookup before each queued Patch.
If the numeric keypad does not appear, set the text input's Format to Number.

faqs.question: How do I design a Power Apps form for phones?
faqs.answer: Use the phone layout, one column, large touch targets, as few inputs as possible, and buttons in place of small drop-downs.

faqs.question: Can field staff save updates without signal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Store the update in a collection with SaveData and send it when Connection.Connected is true again.

faqs.question: How do I record where an update was made?
faqs.answer: Read Location.Latitude and Location.Longitude at save time and store them with the update.

create-a-checklist-review-experience.shortDescription: A screen for working through a checklist against a record: items grouped by section, pass, fail or not applicable per item, a comment on failures, progress shown and one save.
create-a-checklist-review-experience.fullDescription: Inspections, quality gates and onboarding reviews are all checklists answered against one record. The experience should let a reviewer move down the list quickly, mark each item, explain failures and see how far they have got. Answers are held in a collection while working and written in one operation, with the template kept in its own list so it can change without editing the app.
create-a-checklist-review-experience.problemStatement: Reviewers fill in a spreadsheet copy of the checklist for each inspection. Versions drift, failures have no comments, and nobody can report which items fail most often.
whenToUse: Inspections, audits, release gates and onboarding reviews
Checklists of 10 to 80 items answered against a record
Templates that change over time
whenNotToUse: Two or three yes/no questions, which fit as columns on the record
Checklists needing photos and signatures per item on mobile, which call for a dedicated inspection app
create-a-checklist-review-experience.formulaOrCode:
Lists
  Checklist Templates:  Title (item text), Section, SortOrder, TemplateName, Active (yes/no), Guidance (text)
  Checklist Answers:    Title, ReviewId (number), TemplateItemId (number), Section, Result (choice: Pass, Fail, NA),
                        Comment (multi-line)
  Reviews:              Title, Subject (what is being reviewed), Reviewer, Status (Draft, Complete), Score (number)

Load the working set (screen OnVisible)
  ClearCollect(colItems,
      AddColumns(
          SortByColumns(Filter('Checklist Templates', TemplateName = gblReview.TemplateName, Active), "SortOrder"),
          Result, "", Comment, "", AnswerId, 0));
  // Bring back saved answers when reopening a draft
  ForAll(Filter('Checklist Answers', ReviewId = gblReview.ID) As a,
      UpdateIf(colItems, ID = a.TemplateItemId, { Result: a.Result.Value, Comment: a.Comment, AnswerId: a.ID }))

Gallery (galItems, flexible height)
  Items: colItems
  Section header: show the section label only on its first row
    lblSection.Visible: ThisItem.ID = First(Filter(colItems, Section = ThisItem.Section)).ID
  Row: item text, guidance (subtle), three buttons, comment box

  Result buttons (one of three)
    btnPass.OnSelect: Patch(colItems, ThisItem, { Result: "Pass" })
    btnFail.OnSelect: Patch(colItems, ThisItem, { Result: "Fail" })
    btnNA.OnSelect:   Patch(colItems, ThisItem, { Result: "NA" })
    btnPass.Fill: If(ThisItem.Result = "Pass", ColorValue("#107C10"), ColorValue("#F3F2F1"))
    btnFail.Fill: If(ThisItem.Result = "Fail", ColorValue("#D13438"), ColorValue("#F3F2F1"))
    Add text or an icon as well as colour: "Pass", "Fail", "N/A".

  Comment (shown and required on Fail)
    txtComment.Visible: ThisItem.Result = "Fail"
    txtComment.Default: ThisItem.Comment
    txtComment.OnChange: Patch(colItems, ThisItem, { Comment: Self.Text })
    BorderColor: If(ThisItem.Result = "Fail" && IsBlank(ThisItem.Comment), Color.Red, ColorValue("#8A8886"))

Progress and score
  locAnswered = CountRows(Filter(colItems, Result <> ""))
  Label: locAnswered & " of " & CountRows(colItems) & " answered"
  Progress bar width: Parent.Width * locAnswered / Max(1, CountRows(colItems))
  Score: With({ scored: Filter(colItems, Result in ["Pass", "Fail"]) },
              If(CountRows(scored) = 0, Blank(), Round(CountRows(Filter(scored, Result = "Pass")) / CountRows(scored) * 100, 0)))
  Failures: CountRows(Filter(colItems, Result = "Fail"))

Jump to the next unanswered item
  btnNext.OnSelect: Select(galItems, ...) is not needed. Filter toggle "Show unanswered only":
  galItems.Items: If(tglOpen.Value, Filter(colItems, Result = ""), colItems)

Save (draft or complete)
  btnSave.OnSelect
    UpdateContext({ locSaving: true });
    IfError(
        // new answers
        ForAll(Filter(colItems, Result <> "", AnswerId = 0) As i,
            Patch('Checklist Answers', Defaults('Checklist Answers'),
                  { Title: Left(i.Title, 250), ReviewId: gblReview.ID, TemplateItemId: i.ID, Section: i.Section,
                    Result: { Value: i.Result }, Comment: i.Comment }));
        // changed answers
        ForAll(Filter(colItems, AnswerId > 0) As i,
            Patch('Checklist Answers', LookUp('Checklist Answers', ID = i.AnswerId),
                  { Result: { Value: i.Result }, Comment: i.Comment }));
        Patch(Reviews, gblReview, { Score: locScore, Status: { Value: If(locComplete, "Complete", "Draft") } }),
        Notify("Save failed: " & FirstError.Message, NotificationType.Error),
        Notify("Review saved", NotificationType.Success));
    UpdateContext({ locSaving: false })

  Complete is allowed when every item is answered and every failure has a comment:
    locComplete = CountRows(Filter(colItems, Result = "")) = 0 &&
                  CountRows(Filter(colItems, Result = "Fail" && IsBlank(Comment))) = 0
  After completion, show the gallery read-only: buttons DisplayMode: If(gblReview.Status.Value = "Complete", Disabled, Edit)

Reporting
  Because answers are rows, a view or report can count Fail by TemplateItemId to find the weakest items.
stepByStepInstructions: Create lists for checklist templates, answers and reviews.
Load the template items into a collection with result and comment columns.
Show items in a gallery grouped by section with pass, fail and not-applicable buttons.
Require a comment for each failed item.
Show answered count, score and failures as the reviewer works.
Write new and changed answers in one save and lock the review when complete.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding checklist items into the app.
Writing to the data source on every tap.
Colour as the only sign of pass or fail.
Allowing completion with unanswered items or uncommented failures.
troubleshooting: If reopened drafts lose answers, check the UpdateIf that merges saved answers matches on the template item ID.
If saving is slow, write only new and changed rows, not every item.
If section headers repeat, compare each row's ID with the first row of its section.
If the comment box loses text, set its Default from the collection and save on change.

faqs.question: How do I build a checklist in Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Keep items in a template list, load them into a collection, mark each in a gallery and save the answers as rows linked to the review.

faqs.question: How do I require a comment for failed items?
faqs.answer: Show the comment box when the result is Fail and block completion while any failed item has an empty comment.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a checklist score?
faqs.answer: Divide the number of passes by the number of items marked pass or fail, leaving out not-applicable items.

create-a-data-quality-repair-panel.shortDescription: A panel that lists records failing data-quality rules, shows what is wrong with each and lets a data steward fix the value inline, with every correction logged.
create-a-data-quality-repair-panel.fullDescription: Bad rows get into lists through imports, grid edits and old versions of forms. Hunting for them one view at a time does not scale. A repair panel runs a set of named checks, counts the failures, lists the affected records with the reason, and gives a quick fix for each, so cleaning data becomes a routine task instead of a project.
create-a-data-quality-repair-panel.problemStatement: Reports are wrong because some requests have no category, some have end dates before start dates and some have owners who left. Nobody knows how many, and fixing them means opening items one by one.
whenToUse: Lists that feed reports or automation and suffer from missing or inconsistent values
A named data steward who fixes records regularly
After migrations and bulk imports
whenNotToUse: Problems that should be prevented with validation, which is the better fix where possible
Bulk corrections of thousands of rows, which suit a flow or script
create-a-data-quality-repair-panel.formulaOrCode:
Rules, defined once (App.Formulas)
  nfRules = Table(
    { Id: "nocat",   Label: "No category",                 Fix: "Choose a category" },
    { Id: "dates",   Label: "End date before start date",  Fix: "Correct the dates" },
    { Id: "noowner", Label: "No owner",                    Fix: "Assign an owner" },
    { Id: "stale",   Label: "Open and untouched 90+ days", Fix: "Close or update" },
    { Id: "title",   Label: "Title shorter than 5 characters", Fix: "Rewrite the title" }
  );

Load and evaluate (button "Run checks", or screen OnVisible)
  ClearCollect(colRows, Filter(Requests, Status.Value <> "Closed"));        // delegable part first
  ClearCollect(colIssues,
      ForAll(Filter(colRows, IsBlank(Category.Value)),                 { RuleId: "nocat",   RowId: ID, Title: Title }),
      ForAll(Filter(colRows, !IsBlank(EndDate) && EndDate < StartDate), { RuleId: "dates",   RowId: ID, Title: Title }),
      ForAll(Filter(colRows, IsBlank(Owner.Email)),                    { RuleId: "noowner", RowId: ID, Title: Title }),
      ForAll(Filter(colRows, Modified < DateAdd(Today(), -90, TimeUnit.Days)), { RuleId: "stale", RowId: ID, Title: Title }),
      ForAll(Filter(colRows, Len(Trim(Title)) < 5),                    { RuleId: "title",   RowId: ID, Title: Title }));
  Set(locCheckedAt, Now())
  The checks run on the collection, so non-delegable tests are fine. Keep the first Filter delegable and
  under the 2,000 row limit, or run per status or per year.

Summary (galRules)
  Items: AddColumns(nfRules, Count, CountRows(Filter(colIssues, RuleId = Id)))
  Row: Label, Count badge (red when above 0).   OnSelect: Set(locRule, ThisItem.Id)
  Header: CountRows(colIssues) & " issues in " & CountRows(colRows) & " open records, checked " & Text(locCheckedAt, "hh:mm")

Affected records (galIssues)
  Items: Filter(colIssues, RuleId = locRule)
  Row: Title, link to open the full record, and the fix control for the selected rule.

Fix controls by rule (visible according to locRule)
  nocat:   drpCategory (Items: Choices(Requests.Category))  + btnApply
     Patch(Requests, LookUp(Requests, ID = ThisItem.RowId), { Category: drpCategory.Selected })
  noowner: cmbOwner (people)  + btnApply
     Patch(Requests, LookUp(Requests, ID = ThisItem.RowId), { Owner: cmbOwner.Selected })
  dates:   two date pickers preset to the current values
  stale:   buttons "Close" and "Still active" (the second just touches a ReviewedOn date)
  title:   text input preset to the current title

Apply with a log entry and remove the issue from the panel
  btnApply.OnSelect
    IfError(
        Patch(Requests, LookUp(Requests, ID = ThisItem.RowId), { Category: drpCategory.Selected });
        Patch('Data Fix Log', Defaults('Data Fix Log'),
              { Title: "Request " & ThisItem.RowId, Rule: locRule, OldValue: "(blank)",
                NewValue: drpCategory.Selected.Value, FixedBy: User().Email, FixedOn: Now() }),
        Notify("Not fixed: " & FirstError.Message, NotificationType.Error),
        Remove(colIssues, ThisItem); Notify("Fixed", NotificationType.Success))

Fix all for a rule with one value (use sparingly)
  btnFixAll.OnSelect (after a confirmation dialog)
    ForAll(Filter(colIssues, RuleId = "nocat") As i,
        Patch(Requests, LookUp(Requests, ID = i.RowId), { Category: drpBulkCategory.Selected }));
    RemoveIf(colIssues, RuleId = "nocat")

Access
  Show the screen only to stewards:  LookUp('App Roles', Email = User().Email).Role = "Steward"
  and make sure list permissions agree. Hiding a screen is not security.

Stop the problem at source
  For each rule with a steady stream of new failures, add list validation, a required column or a form rule.
  Track counts per rule per week: a 'Data Quality Snapshot' list written by "Run checks" shows whether
  prevention is working.
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the data-quality rules with the list owner and name each one.
Load the open records with a delegable filter into a collection.
Evaluate each rule against the collection and build an issues collection.
Show a count per rule and the affected records for the selected rule.
Provide an inline fix per rule that patches the record, writes a log row and removes the issue.
Add validation at the source for rules that keep producing failures.
commonMistakes: Fixing data repeatedly without preventing the cause.
Running non-delegable checks straight against a large list.
No record of who changed what.
A fix-all button with no confirmation.
troubleshooting: If counts look low, the first filter hit the row limit. Narrow it and run in batches.
If a fix succeeds but the issue remains, remove it from the issues collection after the Patch.
If the people picker patch fails, pass the selected person record from a combo box bound to the column's choices.
If stewards cannot save, check their list permissions, not just the screen's visibility.

faqs.question: How do I find bad data in a SharePoint list with Power Apps?
faqs.answer: Load the records into a collection, run named checks against it and collect the failing rows with the rule they broke.

faqs.question: Should data fixes be logged?
faqs.answer: Yes. Write a log row with the record, rule, old and new value, who fixed it and when.

faqs.question: How do I stop bad data returning?
faqs.answer: Add validation or required settings at the list for each rule that keeps failing.

create-a-reusable-app-settings-panel.shortDescription: A settings panel component you can drop into any canvas app: user preferences such as default view, page size and theme, saved per user and applied at start-up.
create-a-reusable-app-settings-panel.fullDescription: Users ask for small preferences: start on my items, show 25 rows, use the compact layout. Hard-coding one choice suits nobody. A settings panel built as a component, backed by a per-user settings list, gives every app the same slide-in panel and the same way of reading preferences, with defaults when a user has never opened it.
create-a-reusable-app-settings-panel.problemStatement: Each app handles preferences differently or not at all. Users reset their filters every session, and makers rebuild a settings screen for each new app.
whenToUse: Apps used daily where users want their own defaults
Several apps that should offer the same preference panel
Per-user options: default tab, page size, density, notifications
