  Export the list schema (PnP template or the columns page) and store it with the date as the new baseline.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the schema change requests list with change type, detail, consumers, impact and decision.
Publish the risk guide so requesters can rate impact themselves.
Maintain a register of which apps, flows and reports use each list.
Meet weekly to walk through proposed changes with the review questions.
Require a tested copy and rollback plan for high-impact changes.
After each change, verify every consumer and store the new schema baseline.
commonMistakes: Treating a column type change as a quick edit.
Reviewing the change but not who updates the consumers.
A board so heavy that people bypass it.
No record of the schema before the change.
troubleshooting: If an app shows errors after a change, refresh the data source in the app and correct formulas that used the old name.
If a flow fails on a missing field, reopen the action so it reloads the list's columns.
If a type change is unavoidable, add a new column, copy the data, switch consumers, then retire the old column.
If people skip the board, allow low-impact approvals in the channel.

faqs.question: Why review SharePoint list schema changes?
faqs.answer: Apps, flows and reports depend on column names and types, so an unreviewed change can break them for users.

faqs.question: Is renaming a SharePoint column safe?
faqs.answer: Renaming the display name keeps the internal name, so flows usually continue, but Power Apps formulas using the old display name need updating.

faqs.question: How do I change a column's type safely?
faqs.answer: Add a new column of the right type, copy the data across, repoint apps and flows, then remove the old column.

create-a-site-launch-communication-plan.shortDescription: A communication plan for launching a SharePoint site: audiences, messages, channels, dates and owners from first announcement to the follow-up a month later.
create-a-site-launch-communication-plan.fullDescription: A site launched with one email on the day gets a spike of visits and then silence. A communication plan staggers the message: sponsors first, then champions, then everyone, with different content for people who must change how they work and people who only need to know. It also covers where questions go and what happens to the old location.
create-a-site-launch-communication-plan.problemStatement: A new intranet site goes live. Half the organisation hears about it from a broken bookmark, managers cannot answer questions and the old site keeps getting updated.
whenToUse: New intranet, department or project sites replacing an older location
Launches that change where people find or store things
Any site whose success depends on adoption
whenNotToUse: A team site for five people who built it together
Governing how ongoing site changes are announced, which is a separate standard
create-a-site-launch-communication-plan.formulaOrCode:
SITE LAUNCH COMMUNICATION PLAN      Site: ____________   Launch date (L): ________   Comms owner: ________

1. Audiences
   Audience            Size    What changes for them                      What they need
   Sponsors            5       Accountable for adoption                   Talking points, date, success measures
   Content owners      20      Must publish in the new site               Training, deadlines, freeze dates
   Managers            60      Will be asked questions                    One-page brief, FAQ
   Champions           15      First line of help                         Early access, demo, support channel
   All staff           1,200   New place to find things                   What, when, where, why, help
   Service desk        10      Will get tickets                           Known issues, routing, FAQ

2. Key messages (agree once, reuse everywhere)
   What:   "<Site name> replaces <old site> from <date>."
   Why:    one benefit in the reader's terms: "Find policies in one search" not "modern architecture".
   Action: what to do: update bookmarks, use the new request form, stop saving to the old library.
   Help:   one link and one channel.

3. Timeline
   When     Audience         Channel                    Message                               Owner
   L-28     Sponsors         Meeting + one-pager        Date, scope, their role               Project lead
   L-21     Content owners   Workshop + email           Publishing steps, content freeze L-5  Site owner
   L-14     Champions        Teams session + early access  Tour, feedback, how to help        Comms owner
   L-10     Managers         Email + brief              What your team will see, FAQ          Sponsor
   L-7      All staff        Intranet news + Viva Engage/Teams post   "Coming next week", 60-second video   Comms owner
   L-5      Content owners   Email                      Content freeze on old site begins     Site owner
   L-1      Service desk     Briefing                   Known issues, routing                 Support lead
   L        All staff        Email from sponsor + news post + banner on old site   It is live: link, three things to try   Sponsor
   L        Champions        Teams channel              Floor-walking, collect questions      Comms owner
   L+2      All staff        Teams post                 Top five questions answered           Comms owner
   L+7      All staff        News post                  Tips, what we fixed, old site read-only date   Site owner
   L+14     Managers         Email                      Usage so far, reminder on old links   Sponsor
   L+30     All staff        News post + survey         What we learned, old site retired     Comms owner

4. Assets to prepare (with owners and due dates)
   [ ] One-page brief for managers            [ ] FAQ page on the new site
   [ ] Launch news post and email             [ ] 60-second tour video or annotated screenshots
   [ ] Banner text for the old site           [ ] Redirects or a "we have moved" page
   [ ] Champion guide                         [ ] Service desk notes
   [ ] Feedback form                          [ ] Teams or Viva Engage channel for questions

5. Old location
   L-5: content freeze.   L: banner "This site has moved" with the link.   L+7: read-only.
   L+30: redirect or remove from navigation and search.   State these dates in every message.

6. Feedback and support
   Questions: #new-site-help channel, monitored by champions 09:00 to 17:00 for two weeks.
   Feedback form linked from the site footer. Review daily in week one, weekly after.
   Log issues in the launch list and publish "you said, we did" at L+7 and L+30.

7. Measures
   Reach:     email opens, news post views.
   Adoption:  site visits and unique viewers (Site usage) at L+7 and L+30 against the old site's baseline.
   Behaviour: visits to the old site falling, searches landing on new pages, tickets per week.
   Sentiment: three-question survey at L+30.

8. Risks
   Launch date moves: every message has an owner who can hold it. Avoid dates in pre-recorded video.
   Message fatigue: no more than two all-staff messages in launch week.
   Wrong audience: test distribution lists a week before.
stepByStepInstructions: List the audiences, what changes for each and what they need.
Agree the key messages: what, why, action and help.
Build the timeline from four weeks before launch to thirty days after, with channels and owners.
Prepare the assets, including the manager brief, FAQ and old-site banner.
Set the dates for freezing, redirecting and retiring the old location and repeat them in each message.
Run a help channel and feedback form, and measure reach and adoption at one week and one month.
commonMistakes: One announcement on launch day and nothing after.
The same message for content owners and general staff.
Saying nothing about the old site.
No place for questions, so they go to the project lead's inbox.
troubleshooting: If visits drop after week one, publish tips and answer the top questions in a follow-up post.
If the old site keeps being used, add the banner, make it read-only and redirect key pages.
If managers cannot answer questions, send the one-page brief again with the FAQ link.
If the date slips, update the banner and timeline first, then send a short correction.

faqs.question: What should a site launch communication plan include?
faqs.answer: Audiences, key messages, a dated timeline of messages by channel and owner, assets, plans for the old site, support and measures.

faqs.question: When should I announce a new SharePoint site?
faqs.answer: Brief sponsors and content owners three to four weeks ahead, tell all staff a week before, announce on the day and follow up at one week and one month.

faqs.question: How do I measure a site launch?
faqs.answer: Compare site visits and unique viewers with the old site's baseline, and track questions, tickets and a short survey after a month.

create-a-conditional-approval-flow.shortDescription: A Power Automate approval that decides at run time whether approval is needed, who approves and how many stages run, from rules held in a list instead of nested conditions.
create-a-conditional-approval-flow.fullDescription: Most approval flows start simple and collect conditions: over a limit add finance, for IT purchases add security, under a small amount skip approval. Encoding each rule as a branch makes the flow unreadable. This pattern evaluates the request against a rules list, builds an ordered array of approval stages and runs them in one loop, so adding a rule is a list edit.
create-a-conditional-approval-flow.problemStatement: An approval flow has six nested conditions and four copies of the approval action. Changing the finance limit means editing three branches, and nobody is sure which path a 4,900 request takes.
whenToUse: Approvals where the route depends on amount, category, department or risk
Rules that change several times a year
Processes where small requests should be auto-approved
whenNotToUse: A single fixed approver, where one approval action is enough
Routing on one field only, which a Switch handles clearly
create-a-conditional-approval-flow.formulaOrCode:
Rules list: Approval Rules
  Title            Rule name
  Stage            Number: order of the stage (10, 20, 30)
  Field            Choice: Amount, Category, Department, Risk, Always
  Operator         Choice: ge, lt, eq, ne
  CompareValue     Single line: 5000, IT, High
  ApproverType     Choice: Manager, Person, Group mailbox
  Approver         Person or email (blank for Manager)
  ApprovalType     Choice: First to respond, Everyone must approve
  Active           Yes/No
  Examples
    Auto-approve small      (no rule matches below 250 -> zero stages -> auto-approve)
    Manager        Stage 10  Amount ge 250          Manager
    Finance        Stage 20  Amount ge 5000         finance.approvals@contoso.com
    Security       Stage 20  Category eq IT         it.security@contoso.com
    Director       Stage 30  Amount ge 25000        Person: director

Flow: when an item is created (Requests), trigger condition: @equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/Status/Value'], 'Submitted')

1. Get items (Approval Rules)   Filter Query: Active eq 1    Order By: Stage asc
2. Initialize variable  varStages (Array) = []
3. Initialize variable  varOutcome (String) = 'Approved'
4. Apply to each rule (concurrency 1)
   Compose "Left":  if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Field/Value'],'Amount'), string(triggerOutputs()?['body/Amount']),
                    if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Field/Value'],'Category'), triggerOutputs()?['body/Category/Value'],
                    if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Field/Value'],'Department'), triggerOutputs()?['body/Department/Value'],
                    if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Field/Value'],'Risk'), triggerOutputs()?['body/Risk/Value'], ''))))
   Compose "Matches":
     if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Field/Value'],'Always'), true,
     if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Operator/Value'],'ge'), greaterOrEquals(float(outputs('Left')), float(items('Each_rule')?['CompareValue'])),
     if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Operator/Value'],'lt'), less(float(outputs('Left')), float(items('Each_rule')?['CompareValue'])),
     if(equals(items('Each_rule')?['Operator/Value'],'eq'), equals(toLower(outputs('Left')), toLower(items('Each_rule')?['CompareValue'])),
        not(equals(toLower(outputs('Left')), toLower(items('Each_rule')?['CompareValue'])))))))
   Condition: Matches is true -> Append to varStages:
     { "stage": @{items('Each_rule')?['Stage']}, "name": "@{items('Each_rule')?['Title']}",
       "type": "@{items('Each_rule')?['ApproverType/Value']}", "approver": "@{items('Each_rule')?['Approver/Email']}",
       "mode": "@{items('Each_rule')?['ApprovalType/Value']}" }

5. Condition: length(variables('varStages')) equals 0
   Yes -> Update item: Status = Approved, ApprovalNote = 'Auto-approved: no approval rule applied'. Terminate (Succeeded).

6. Apply to each stage (varStages, concurrency 1)
   a. Condition: varOutcome equals 'Approved'   (skip remaining stages after a rejection)
   b. Compose "AssignedTo":
        if(equals(items('Each_stage')?['type'],'Manager'), body('Get_manager_(V2)')?['mail'], items('Each_stage')?['approver'])
      (Get manager (V2) for the requester runs once before the loop, inside a scope with a fallback approver.)
   c. Start and wait for an approval
        Type: if mode is 'Everyone must approve' use that type, otherwise First to respond
        Title: @{items('Each_stage')?['name']} approval: @{triggerOutputs()?['body/Title']}
        Assigned to: outputs('AssignedTo')
        Details: amount, category, requester, link to the item, and the stages already approved
   d. Create item in Approval History: request ID, stage name, approver, outcome, comments, utcNow()
   e. Condition: outcome is not 'Approve' -> Set varOutcome = 'Rejected'

7. Update item: Status = varOutcome, with the final stage and date. Notify the requester.

Notes
  Stages with the same Stage number run one after another in this design. To run them in parallel, group
  varStages by stage and use a parallel branch or a child flow per group.
  Self-approval: if AssignedTo equals the requester, replace it with the next manager up or a fallback.
  Log varStages on the item (a text column) so anyone can see why a route was chosen.
  Test table: keep ten sample requests with the stages each should produce and re-run them after rule edits.
stepByStepInstructions: Create an Approval Rules list with stage, field, operator, compare value and approver columns.
In the flow, load active rules ordered by stage.
Evaluate each rule against the request and append matching stages to an array.
Auto-approve when no stage applies.
Loop through the stages in order, running an approval for each and stopping after a rejection.
Write each decision to a history list and the route taken to the request.
commonMistakes: Nested conditions with a copy of the approval action in each branch.
Thresholds hard-coded in the flow.
No rule for the requester being their own approver.
Running the stage loop in parallel, so order is lost.
troubleshooting: If numeric comparisons fail, convert both sides with float and make sure the compare value has no currency symbol.
If stages run out of order, set the loop's concurrency to 1 and sort rules by stage.
If the manager lookup fails, wrap it in a scope and fall back to a default approver.
If a rule never matches, compare lower-case values and check for trailing spaces in the rules list.

faqs.question: How do I make an approval conditional in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Evaluate the request against rules first, build the list of stages that apply, and run an approval only for those stages.

faqs.question: How do I skip approval for small requests?
faqs.answer: If no approval rule matches, update the item to approved with a note and end the flow.

faqs.question: Where should approval thresholds be stored?
faqs.answer: In a rules list or environment variables, so they can change without editing the flow.

create-a-daily-exception-digest.shortDescription: A scheduled flow that gathers the day's exceptions from several checks (overdue, missing data, failed runs, stuck approvals) into one email with a section per check, sent only when there is something to report.
create-a-daily-exception-digest.fullDescription: Individual alerts for every exception train people to ignore them. A daily digest runs a defined set of checks each morning, lists what each found and sends one message to the team that can act. The checks are built as parallel branches that each produce a small HTML section, so adding a check does not touch the others.
create-a-daily-exception-digest.problemStatement: A team mailbox receives forty separate alert emails a day from five flows. The one that mattered, a payment stuck for a week, is somewhere in the middle and is missed.
whenToUse: Operational teams watching several lists or processes
Exceptions that can wait until the next morning
Replacing a stream of per-item alerts
whenNotToUse: Incidents that need action within minutes, which need an immediate alert
A digest of one list grouped by owner, which is a simpler single-query flow
create-a-daily-exception-digest.formulaOrCode:
Trigger: Recurrence, every weekday 07:30, with the time zone set. Frequency Week, On these days Mon to Fri, At these hours 7, At these minutes 30. Variables varSections (Array) = [] varTotal (Integer) = 0 Compose "Today": formatDateTime(convertFromUtc(utcNow(), 'GMT Standard Time'), 'yyyy-MM-dd') Compose "Since": addDays(utcNow(), -1) Checks: one Scope per check, all in parallel branches after the variables. Each scope ends by appending { "title", "count", "html" } to varSections. Scope A: Overdue requests Get items (Requests) Filter Query: DueDate lt '@{outputs('Today')}' and Status ne 'Closed' Top Count 100 Select: Request -> item()?['Title'], Owner -> item()?['AssignedTo/DisplayName'], Due -> formatDateTime(item()?['DueDate'],'dd MMM'), Days overdue -> div(sub(ticks(utcNow()),ticks(item()?['DueDate'])),864000000000) Create HTML table (from Select) Append to varSections: { "title": "Overdue requests", "count": @{length(body('Get_overdue')?['value'])}, "html": "@{body('Overdue_table')}" } Scope B: Missing metadata Get items Filter Query: (CostCentre eq null or Category eq null) and Status ne 'Draft' Scope C: Approvals pending more than 3 days Get items (Requests) Filter Query: Status eq 'Pending approval' and SubmittedOn lt '@{addDays(utcNow(),-3)}' Scope D: Failed flow runs since yesterday Get items (Flow Run Log) Filter Query: Outcome eq 'Failed' and Created ge '@{outputs('Since')}' Scope E: Records stuck in an integration state Get items Filter Query: SyncStatus eq 'Error' A failing check must not stop the digest After each scope add an action that runs only when the scope has failed or timed out and appends: { "title": "Overdue requests", "count": -1, "html": "

This check could not run.

" } Assemble (after all branches join; set run-after on the next action to succeeded, failed, skipped, timed out) Filter array "WithResults": varSections where item()?['count'] is not equal to 0 Condition: length(body('WithResults')) is greater than 0 (No -> Terminate, Succeeded: nothing to report) Select "SectionHtml" (text mode) from sort(body('WithResults'),'title'): concat('

', item()?['title'], ' (', if(equals(item()?['count'],-1),'check failed',string(item()?['count'])), ')

', item()?['html']) Compose "Body":

Exceptions for @{formatDateTime(outputs('Today'),'dddd d MMMM')}

@{join(body('SummaryLine'),' | ')}

@{join(body('SectionHtml'),'')}

Sent by the Daily exception digest flow. Reply to this mailbox for changes.

SummaryLine: Select (text mode): concat(item()?['title'], ': ', string(item()?['count'])) Table styling (one Compose applied to the body) replace(replace(replace(outputs('Body'), '','
'), '
',''), '','') Send Send an email from a shared mailbox (V2) To: ops-team@contoso.com Subject: Exception digest @{outputs('Today')}: @{length(body('WithResults'))} areas need attention Optional: Post the summary line to a Teams channel with a link to each list view. Keep a history (optional list "Digest History") Date, check title, count. A chart of counts per check shows whether exceptions are falling. Limits Cap each check at 50 or 100 rows and add "showing the first 50" when the count hits the cap, with a link to a list view that shows everything.
stepByStepInstructions: List the exception checks, the query for each and who acts on them.
Create a weekday recurrence with the time zone set.
Build one scope per check in parallel branches, each producing a title, count and HTML table.
Add a failure path per scope so a broken check is reported instead of stopping the flow.
Combine the sections that found something and end quietly when none did.
Send one styled email from a shared mailbox and optionally log the counts.
commonMistakes: Sending an empty digest every day.
Running checks in sequence so one failure hides the rest.
Unlimited rows in the email.
Sending from a personal account.
troubleshooting: If the digest arrives an hour out in summer, set the time zone on the recurrence instead of using UTC hours.
If sections are missing, check the run-after settings on the action that follows the parallel branches.
If the HTML shows escaped tags, build sections as text and avoid double-encoding in the append step.
If date filters return nothing, format the date as yyyy-MM-dd and wrap it in single quotes.

faqs.question: How do I send a daily summary email from Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use a recurrence trigger, run Get items for each check, build HTML tables with Select and Create HTML table, and send one email.

faqs.question: How do I avoid sending an empty digest?
faqs.answer: Count the results after the checks and terminate the flow when every count is zero.

faqs.question: How do I stop one failed check breaking the digest?
faqs.answer: Put each check in its own scope on a parallel branch and add a run-after failure step that records the check as failed.

create-a-renewal-reminder-workflow.shortDescription: An end-to-end renewal workflow for contracts, licences or certificates: staged reminders, an owner decision to renew or let lapse, escalation when nobody answers and a record of the outcome.
create-a-renewal-reminder-workflow.fullDescription: Reminder emails alone do not renew anything. A renewal workflow tracks each item through stages: upcoming, decision requested, renewing, renewed or lapsed. A daily flow moves items between stages, asks the owner for a decision with a button, escalates silence and rolls the dates forward when the renewal completes.
create-a-renewal-reminder-workflow.problemStatement: A software licence renews automatically at a higher price because the reminder went to someone on leave. Another contract lapses because three reminders were read and nobody was asked to decide anything.
whenToUse: Contracts, subscriptions, certificates, insurance and domain renewals
Items with notice periods where a late decision costs money
Portfolios of 20 to a few thousand renewals
whenNotToUse: A single date reminder with no decision, which a simple reminder flow covers
Renewals managed inside a contract management system that already does this
create-a-renewal-reminder-workflow.formulaOrCode:
List: Renewals
  Title, Supplier, Owner (person), BackupOwner (person), Category (Contract, Licence, Certificate, Insurance),
  RenewalDate (date, indexed), NoticeDays (number: days of notice needed to cancel), TermMonths (number),
  AnnualValue (currency), AutoRenews (yes/no),
  Stage (choice, indexed): Active, Decision requested, Renewing, Renewed, Lapsed, Cancelled
  Decision (choice): Renew, Renegotiate, Cancel         DecisionBy (person)   DecisionOn (date)
  DecisionDeadline (calculated): =[RenewalDate]-[NoticeDays]
  LastReminder (date)   ReminderCount (number)   Notes

Lead time by value (how early to ask)
  Compose "LeadDays":  if(greaterOrEquals(item value, 50000), 120, if(greaterOrEquals(item value, 5000), 90, 60))
  The decision request goes out LeadDays before the DecisionDeadline, not the renewal date.

Flow 1: Daily renewal run (Recurrence 07:00, time zone set)
  Compose "Today": formatDateTime(utcNow(),'yyyy-MM-dd')

  Step A: open decision requests
    Get items: Stage eq 'Active' and RenewalDate le '@{addDays(utcNow(),200,'yyyy-MM-dd')}'
    Filter array: where addDays(item()?['DecisionDeadline'], mul(-1, <LeadDays>)) <= utcNow()
    For each: Update item Stage = 'Decision requested', LastReminder = today, ReminderCount = 1
              Post adaptive card to the Owner (Teams, wait for response is NOT used; a second flow handles the reply)
              or send an email with options (see Flow 2).

  Step B: chase undecided items
    Get items: Stage eq 'Decision requested'
    For each, days to deadline = div(sub(ticks(item()?['DecisionDeadline']), ticks(utcNow())), 864000000000)
      Condition: LastReminder older than 7 days            -> remind Owner, ReminderCount + 1
      Condition: ReminderCount ge 2                         -> copy BackupOwner
      Condition: days to deadline le 14                     -> escalate to the Owner's manager (Get manager V2)
      Condition: days to deadline lt 0 and AutoRenews = No  -> Stage = 'Lapsed', notify owner and procurement
      Condition: days to deadline lt 0 and AutoRenews = Yes -> Stage = 'Renewing', note "auto-renewed without decision", notify

  Step C: complete renewals in progress
    Get items: Stage eq 'Renewing' and RenewalDate le '@{outputs('Today')}'
    Reminder to the owner to confirm the new term (button: Confirm renewed).

Flow 2: Capture the decision
  Option 1: Send email with options (Office 365 Outlook): "Renew", "Renegotiate", "Cancel", in an Apply to each with
            concurrency so each item waits independently; or a child flow per item.
  Option 2: Buttons linking to a small canvas app or list form: .../DispForm.aspx?ID=@{items('Each')?['ID']}
  On decision (trigger: when an item is modified, trigger condition on Decision not empty and Stage 'Decision requested'):
    Renew        -> Stage 'Renewing', create a procurement task (Planner) due by DecisionDeadline
    Renegotiate  -> Stage 'Renewing', task for procurement with 30 days more lead
    Cancel       -> Stage 'Cancelled', task "Send cancellation notice before @{DecisionDeadline}" with the supplier's notice terms
    Record DecisionBy = modified by, DecisionOn = utcNow()

Flow 3: Roll forward (button in the list or when Stage changes to 'Renewed')
  Create the next cycle in place:
    RenewalDate = addToTime(RenewalDate, TermMonths, 'Month'), Stage = 'Active',
    Decision = null, ReminderCount = 0, AnnualValue = new value
  Copy the completed cycle to a "Renewal History" list first: date, decision, value, who decided.

Views
  Decisions needed      Stage = Decision requested, sorted by DecisionDeadline
  Next 90 days          RenewalDate <= [Today]+90 AND Stage = Active
  Lapsed or auto-renewed without decision   (the failures to learn from)
  By owner              Grouped by Owner, total AnnualValue

Calendar view on RenewalDate gives procurement a month-by-month picture.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the Renewals list with renewal date, notice days, owner, backup, stage and decision columns.
Calculate the decision deadline from the renewal date and notice period.
Run a daily flow that opens decision requests ahead of the deadline based on value.
Chase undecided items weekly, add the backup, then escalate to the manager near the deadline.
Capture the decision and create the procurement or cancellation task.
Roll the item forward to its next term after renewal and keep a history row.
commonMistakes: Reminding on the renewal date instead of the notice deadline.
Reminders that ask for no decision.
One owner with no backup or escalation.
Overwriting dates on renewal with no history.
troubleshooting: If reminders repeat daily, update LastReminder after sending and check it before the next one.
If the calculated deadline is wrong, make sure NoticeDays is a number column, not text.
If an owner has left, the reminder fails. Catch the error and send to the backup.
If decisions are not captured, check the trigger condition on the Decision column of the second flow.

faqs.question: How do I build a contract renewal workflow in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Track each renewal's stage in a list, run a daily flow that requests a decision before the notice deadline, escalates silence and rolls dates forward after renewal.

faqs.question: When should renewal reminders start?
faqs.answer: Before the cancellation notice deadline, not the renewal date: commonly 60 to 120 days ahead depending on value.

faqs.question: What if nobody responds to a renewal reminder?
faqs.answer: Copy the backup owner after the second reminder and escalate to the owner's manager two weeks before the deadline.

create-a-flow-support-log.shortDescription: A support log for production flows: every incident, fix and change recorded against the flow, so the next person can see what went wrong before and what was done.
create-a-flow-support-log.fullDescription: Run history disappears after 28 days and says nothing about what a person did in response. A flow support log is the human record: who noticed the problem, what the cause was, how it was fixed and whether it could happen again. It sits alongside automated run logging and is what a support team reads first when a flow misbehaves.
create-a-flow-support-log.problemStatement: A flow fails with the same connector error every few months. Each time a different person spends an hour diagnosing it, because the last fix lives in someone's memory and a deleted chat.
whenToUse: Production flows supported by more than one person
Teams that hand over support between shifts or staff
Flows subject to audit or change control
whenNotToUse: Automated capture of each run's outcome, which is run logging
Personal flows with a single owner and no dependants
create-a-flow-support-log.formulaOrCode:
List: Flow Support Log
  Title              Short summary: "Invoice approval: SharePoint 429 throttling"
  Flow               Lookup to the Flow Inventory list (name, environment, owner)
  EntryType          Choice: Incident, Change, Maintenance, Observation
  Severity           Choice: 1 Business stopped, 2 Degraded, 3 Minor, 4 Information
  DetectedOn         Date and time
  DetectedBy         Choice: Failure alert, User report, Run history review, Monitoring
  RunLink            Hyperlink to the failed run
  FailedAction       Single line: name of the action that failed
  ErrorText          Multiple lines: status code and message, copied from the run
  Impact             Multiple lines: what users saw, how many items affected
  Cause              Choice: Connection expired, Permissions, Throttling, Data problem, Schema change,
                             Timeout, Logic error, Service outage, Licence or limit, Unknown
  CauseDetail        Multiple lines
  Resolution         Multiple lines: exactly what was done
  ItemsReprocessed   Number
  ResolvedOn         Date and time
  ResolvedBy         Person
  Prevention         Multiple lines: change to stop a repeat, or "none: accepted"
  FollowUpDue        Date
  Status             Choice: Open, Fixed, Monitoring, Closed
  MinutesSpent       Number
  RelatedEntry       Lookup (this list)

Calculated
  HoursToResolve     =IF(ISBLANK([ResolvedOn]),"",ROUND(([ResolvedOn]-[DetectedOn])*24,1))

Views
  Open                 Status <> Closed, sorted by Severity then DetectedOn
  By flow              Grouped by Flow, newest first      (the "what happened before" view)
  Repeat causes        Grouped by Cause, Count
  Follow-ups due       FollowUpDue <= [Today]+7 AND Status <> Closed
  This month           DetectedOn in the current month, for the support review

Start an entry automatically
  In each production flow's error handler (a Catch scope that runs after Try has failed):
    Filter array on result('Try') where status is 'Failed'  -> first failed action
    Create item in Flow Support Log:
      Title:        @{workflow()?['tags']?['flowDisplayName']}: @{first(body('Failed'))?['name']}
      EntryType:    Incident       DetectedBy: Failure alert       Status: Open
      DetectedOn:   @{utcNow()}
      FailedAction: @{first(body('Failed'))?['name']}
      ErrorText:    @{coalesce(first(body('Failed'))?['error']?['message'], string(first(body('Failed'))?['outputs']?['body']))}
      RunLink:      https://make.powerautomate.com/environments/@{workflow()?['tags']?['environmentName']}/flows/@{workflow()?['name']}/runs/@{workflow()?['run']?['name']}
  De-duplicate: before creating, Get items where Flow matches, FailedAction matches and Status eq 'Open'.
  If one exists, increment an Occurrences number on it instead of adding a row.

Working an entry (what the supporter fills in)
  1. Open the run link. Confirm the failed action and error.
  2. Check "By flow" for the same action or cause before diagnosing from scratch.
  3. Fix, then resubmit failed runs or reprocess items. Record how many.
  4. Fill Cause, Resolution and Prevention before closing. "Resubmitted" alone is not a resolution.
  5. Set FollowUpDue if a permanent fix is still needed.

Changes and maintenance
  Log planned edits as EntryType Change with what was changed and why, and connection renewals or owner
  changes as Maintenance. When an incident follows a change, link them with RelatedEntry.

Monthly review (15 minutes)
  Incidents by flow and by cause, hours to resolve, repeats (same flow and cause more than once),
  open follow-ups. Pick the top repeat cause and schedule its prevention.

Retention: keep entries for the life of the flow plus one year. The list is small.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the support log list with flow, type, severity, error, cause, resolution and prevention columns.
Link each entry to the flow inventory so entries group by flow.
Add an error handler to production flows that opens an incident entry with the failed action, error and run link.
De-duplicate open entries for the same flow and action.
Have supporters complete cause, resolution and prevention before closing.
Review the log monthly for repeat causes and schedule permanent fixes.
commonMistakes: Closing entries with only the word resubmitted.
A new row for every failed run of the same problem.
Logging incidents but not changes.
Keeping the log in a chat thread or mailbox.
troubleshooting: If the run link opens the wrong place, build it from the environment name, flow name and run name in workflow().
If error text is blank, read the action's outputs body as well as its error message.
If the handler does not run, set its run-after to has failed and has timed out on the Try scope.
If entries pile up for one outage, check the open-entry lookup before creating.

faqs.question: What is a flow support log?
faqs.answer: A list recording incidents, fixes and changes for production flows, including cause, resolution and prevention, so support knowledge is kept.

faqs.question: How is a support log different from run logging?
faqs.answer: Run logging captures each run's outcome automatically. The support log records what people found and did about problems.

faqs.question: How do I get a link to the failed run?
faqs.answer: Build it from workflow(): the environment name, the flow name and the run name in the Power Automate portal URL.

create-a-teams-escalation-notice.shortDescription: An escalation message posted to a Teams channel when something breaches a threshold, with the facts, an owner mention, an acknowledge button and a follow-up if nobody takes it.
create-a-teams-escalation-notice.fullDescription: An escalation is different from a notification: someone has to own it. The notice is an adaptive card stating what breached, by how much and since when, mentions the on-call person or tag, and carries an Acknowledge action. The flow records who acknowledged and escalates again to the next level if no one does within the agreed time.
create-a-teams-escalation-notice.problemStatement: High-priority tickets that pass their response time trigger a plain channel message. It scrolls away, three people assume someone else has it, and the manager finds out the next morning.
whenToUse: SLA breaches, stuck approvals, failed critical flows and safety or security events
Teams with an on-call rota or a duty tag
Events needing a named owner within minutes or hours
whenNotToUse: Routine status updates, which belong in a normal channel post or digest
Paging outside working hours, which needs a dedicated on-call tool
create-a-teams-escalation-notice.formulaOrCode:
Trigger options
  Scheduled check every 15 minutes: Get items where Priority eq 'High' and Status eq 'New' and
      Created lt '@{addMinutes(utcNow(),-60)}' and Escalated ne 1
  Or event-driven: a monitoring flow calls this as a child flow with { title, detail, link, level, itemId }.

1. Mark the item first (prevents a second notice on the next run)
   Update item: Escalated = Yes, EscalatedOn = utcNow(), EscalationLevel = 1

2. Work out who to mention
   Get item from the "On Call" list for today, or use a Teams tag.
   Get an @mention token for a user (Teams connector): user = on-call person's email
   For a tag, post as a message with <at>Duty team</at> using the tag mention format, or mention the person.

3. Post adaptive card and wait for a response (Flow bot, Channel)
   {
     "type": "AdaptiveCard", "$schema": "http://adaptivecards.io/schemas/adaptive-card.json", "version": "1.4",
     "msteams": { "width": "Full",
       "entities": [ { "type": "mention", "text": "<at>@{outputs('OnCallName')}</at>",
                       "mentioned": { "id": "@{outputs('OnCallEmail')}", "name": "@{outputs('OnCallName')}" } } ] },
     "body": [
       { "type": "Container", "style": "attention", "bleed": true, "items": [
         { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "ESCALATION: response time breached", "weight": "Bolder", "size": "Medium", "wrap": true } ] },
       { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "@{items('Each')?['Title']}", "weight": "Bolder", "wrap": true },
       { "type": "FactSet", "facts": [
         { "title": "Priority", "value": "High" },
         { "title": "Waiting", "value": "@{div(sub(ticks(utcNow()),ticks(items('Each')?['Created'])),600000000)} minutes" },
         { "title": "Target", "value": "60 minutes" },
         { "title": "Requester", "value": "@{items('Each')?['Author/DisplayName']}" },
         { "title": "Level", "value": "1 of 3" } ] },
       { "type": "TextBlock", "text": "<at>@{outputs('OnCallName')}</at> please acknowledge within 15 minutes.", "wrap": true }
     ],
     "actions": [
       { "type": "Action.Submit", "title": "Acknowledge: I own this", "data": { "action": "ack" } },
       { "type": "Action.OpenUrl", "title": "Open item", "url": "@{items('Each')?['{Link}']}" }
     ]
   }
   Action settings > Timeout: PT15M

4. After the card (configure run after: is successful, has timed out)
   Condition: the card action succeeded
     Yes -> Update item: AcknowledgedBy = body('Post_card')?['responder']?['displayName'],
                         AcknowledgedOn = utcNow(), Status = 'Assigned'
            Update message text on the card: "Acknowledged by <name> at <time>"
            Reply in the thread: "@{responder} has this."
     No (timed out) -> Level 2:
            Update item: EscalationLevel = 2
            Post a second card mentioning the team lead (Get manager V2 of the on-call person, or the lead from the On Call list), timeout PT30M
            Still nothing -> Level 3: chat message to the service manager and an email marked high importance.

5. Record
   Create item in "Escalation Log": item ID, level reached, mentioned people, acknowledged by, minutes to acknowledge.
   Weekly view: escalations by reason, median minutes to acknowledge, any that reached level 3.

Design rules
  One notice per breach, updated in place. Replies go in its thread.
  State the number that breached and the target. "Ticket needs attention" is not an escalation.
  Mention one accountable person or tag, never the whole channel.
  Use a dedicated Escalations channel with notifications set to all activity for the duty team.
  Quiet hours: outside the rota's hours, hold the notice until the next start time or route to the on-call tool.
  If the item is resolved while the card is waiting, a separate flow updates the card to "Resolved" using the stored message ID.

Each waiting card holds a flow run open (up to 30 days). For high volumes, post without waiting and handle
the button with the "When someone responds to an adaptive card" trigger instead.
stepByStepInstructions: Define the breach conditions, targets and the three escalation levels with timings.
Detect breaches on a schedule or from a monitoring flow and flag the item as escalated first.
Look up today's on-call person or tag.
Post an adaptive card with the facts, a mention and an Acknowledge button, with a timeout.
On acknowledge, record the owner and update the card. On timeout, escalate to the next level.
Log each escalation and review time to acknowledge weekly.
commonMistakes: Posting the same breach every time the schedule runs.
Mentioning everyone in the channel.
No acknowledge step, so ownership is assumed.
Vague text with no numbers or link.
troubleshooting: If the mention shows as plain text, the at-tag text must match the entity text exactly and the ID must be the user's UPN or object ID.
If the flow does not continue after the timeout, add has timed out to the next action's run-after.
If duplicates appear, set the Escalated flag before posting and filter on it.
If the card fails to post, validate the JSON in the Adaptive Cards designer and check the schema version is 1.4 or lower.

faqs.question: How do I send an escalation to Teams from Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Post an adaptive card to a channel with the breach details, mention the accountable person and include an acknowledge button with a timeout.

faqs.question: How do I escalate again if nobody responds?
faqs.answer: Set a timeout on the post-and-wait action and add a path that runs on timeout to notify the next level.

faqs.question: How do I stop repeated escalation messages?
faqs.answer: Flag the item as escalated before posting and exclude flagged items from the check.

create-a-child-task-creation-flow.shortDescription: A reusable child flow that creates a set of tasks under a parent record from a template, with due dates calculated from offsets, and returns what it created to the caller.
create-a-child-task-creation-flow.fullDescription: Several processes need the same thing: when a parent record reaches a state, create its standard tasks. Building that into each parent flow means the logic is copied and drifts. A child flow takes the parent ID, a template name and a start date, creates the tasks idempotently and returns a count and any failures, so approval, onboarding and project flows can all call it.
create-a-child-task-creation-flow.problemStatement: Three flows each contain their own loop that creates tasks. One skips weekends, one does not, one creates duplicates when re-run, and a change to the task template has to be made in three places.
whenToUse: Standard task sets created after approval, onboarding, intake or stage change
Several parent flows needing the same task logic
Task templates maintained by the business in a list
whenNotToUse: One or two fixed tasks, which the parent flow can create directly
Tasks that belong in Planner with buckets and checklists, where the Planner connector pattern fits
create-a-child-task-creation-flow.formulaOrCode:
Lists
  Task Templates:  Title (task name), TemplateName, Sequence (number), OffsetDays (number, from start date),
                   AssigneeRole (choice: Requester, Owner, Manager, Named), AssigneeEmail, Instructions, Active
  Tasks:           Title, ParentId (number, indexed), ParentList (text), TemplateItemId (number), DueDate,
                   AssignedTo (person), Status (Not started, In progress, Done), Sequence, TaskKey (text, indexed, unique)

Child flow (in a solution): "Create tasks from template"
  Trigger: Manually trigger a flow (inputs)
    ParentId (Number), ParentList (Text), TemplateName (Text), StartDate (Text, yyyy-MM-dd),
    OwnerEmail (Text), RequesterEmail (Text), SkipWeekends (Yes/No)

  1. Initialize varCreated (Integer) = 0;  varSkipped (Integer) = 0;  varErrors (Array) = []

  2. Get items (Task Templates)
       Filter Query: TemplateName eq '@{triggerBody()?['text_1']}' and Active eq 1     Order By: Sequence asc
     Condition: length(value) equals 0 -> Respond { created: 0, status: "NoTemplate" } and Terminate.

  3. Get items (Tasks)   Filter Query: ParentId eq @{triggerBody()?['number']} and ParentList eq '@{triggerBody()?['text']}'
     Select "ExistingKeys": item()?['TaskKey']          (one call, instead of a lookup per task)

  4. Apply to each template row (concurrency 1 keeps the sequence; raise it if order does not matter)
     Compose "Key":  concat(triggerBody()?['text'], '-', string(triggerBody()?['number']), '-', string(items('Each')?['ID']))
     Condition: contains(body('ExistingKeys'), outputs('Key'))
       Yes -> Increment varSkipped
       No  ->
         Compose "RawDue":  addDays(triggerBody()?['text_2'], int(items('Each')?['OffsetDays']))
         Compose "Due" (move weekend dates to Monday when SkipWeekends is true):
           if(and(triggerBody()?['boolean'], equals(dayOfWeek(outputs('RawDue')), 6)), addDays(outputs('RawDue'), 2),
           if(and(triggerBody()?['boolean'], equals(dayOfWeek(outputs('RawDue')), 0)), addDays(outputs('RawDue'), 1),
              outputs('RawDue')))
         Compose "Assignee":
           if(equals(items('Each')?['AssigneeRole/Value'],'Requester'), triggerBody()?['text_4'],
           if(equals(items('Each')?['AssigneeRole/Value'],'Named'), items('Each')?['AssigneeEmail'],
              triggerBody()?['text_3']))
         Scope "Try create"
           Create item (Tasks):
             Title: @{items('Each')?['Title']}       ParentId, ParentList from the inputs
             TemplateItemId: @{items('Each')?['ID']} Sequence: @{items('Each')?['Sequence']}
             DueDate: @{formatDateTime(outputs('Due'),'yyyy-MM-dd')}
             AssignedTo Claims: i:0#.f|membership|@{outputs('Assignee')}
             Status: Not started                    TaskKey: @{outputs('Key')}
           Increment varCreated
         Scope "Catch" (run after Try create has failed)
           Append to varErrors: { "task": "@{items('Each')?['Title']}", "error": "@{coalesce(body('Create_item')?['message'], 'Create failed')}" }

  5. Respond to a Power App or flow
       Created (Number): varCreated      Skipped (Number): varSkipped
       Errors (Text): string(variables('varErrors'))
       Status (Text): if(equals(length(variables('varErrors')),0),'OK','Partial')

  Child flow settings
    Run only users: set every connection to "Use this connection", not "Provided by run-only user".
    The child flow must be in the same solution environment as its parents.

Calling it (parent flow)
  Trigger condition on the parent: @equals(triggerOutputs()?['body/Status/Value'],'Approved')
  Run a Child Flow: ParentId = ID, ParentList = 'Requests', TemplateName = 'Vendor onboarding',
     StartDate = formatDateTime(utcNow(),'yyyy-MM-dd'), OwnerEmail, RequesterEmail, SkipWeekends = Yes
  Condition: Status is not 'OK' -> notify the owner with Errors; else update the parent: TasksCreated = Yes.

Why the key matters
  Trigger retries and manual re-runs happen. TaskKey (parent list, parent ID, template row ID) with
  "Enforce unique values" makes a second run skip what exists and create only what is missing.

Dependent tasks (optional)
  Add PredecessorSequence to the template. Create later tasks with Status "Waiting" and let a small flow on
  task completion release the next one and set its due date from the completion date.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a task template list with sequence, offset days and assignee role.
Add a unique TaskKey column to the Tasks list.
Build the child flow with inputs for parent, template name, start date and people.
Load existing task keys once and skip template rows already created.
Create each task with a calculated due date and assignee, catching failures.
Respond with created, skipped and error details, and call the child from each parent flow.
commonMistakes: Copying the task loop into every parent flow.
No idempotency key, so re-runs duplicate tasks.
Child flow connections left as provided by the run-only user.
Returning nothing, so the parent cannot tell whether tasks were created.
troubleshooting: If the parent cannot find the child flow, both must be in a solution in the same environment.
If the child fails with a connection error, set its run-only user connections to use the embedded connection.
If due dates fall on weekends, check dayOfWeek values: 0 is Sunday and 6 is Saturday.
If the assignee fails to resolve, pass a valid email and use the claims format in the person field.

faqs.question: How do I create multiple tasks from a template in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Keep the tasks in a template list, loop through the rows for the chosen template and create a task per row with a due date offset from a start date.

faqs.question: How do I stop duplicate tasks when a flow re-runs?
faqs.answer: Give each task a unique key built from the parent and template row, and skip keys that already exist.

faqs.question: Why use a child flow for task creation?
faqs.answer: Several parent flows can share one tested implementation, and changes are made in one place.

create-a-service-account-review.shortDescription: A periodic review of the service accounts that own flows and connections: what each account can reach, who knows its credentials, whether MFA and licences are right and which flows depend on it.
create-a-service-account-review.fullDescription: Moving flows to a service account fixes the leaver problem and creates a different one: a shared, highly privileged identity that nobody reviews. A service account review checks each account twice a year for ownership, sign-in protection, licence, the connections it holds and the access those connections give, and removes what is no longer needed.
create-a-service-account-review.problemStatement: A service account created three years ago owns 60 flows, is a site collection admin on a dozen sites, has a password known to six people, two of whom have left, and is excluded from MFA.
whenToUse: Any tenant using shared or service accounts for flows and connections
Before audits or after staff with credential knowledge leave
When deciding whether to move flows to service principals
whenNotToUse: Deciding the ownership model in the first place, which is a governance standard
Flows on personal accounts, which need reassignment first
create-a-service-account-review.formulaOrCode:
Register: Service Accounts (list in the admin or CoE site)
  Title (UPN), Purpose, BusinessOwner (person), TechnicalOwner (person), CredentialLocation (e.g. Key Vault name),
  CredentialHolders (people), LastPasswordChange (date), MfaMethod (choice: Authenticator on shared device,
  FIDO2 key, Certificate, Excluded by policy), InteractiveSignInNeeded (yes/no),
  Licences (text), Environments (text), FlowCount, ConnectionCount, AdminRoles (text),
  LastReviewed (date), NextReview (date), ReviewOutcome (choice: OK, Actions open, Retire), Notes

Review checklist (per account, every 6 months)
  Identity
  [ ] Business owner and technical owner are current staff
  [ ] Account is used by one workload area, not everything in the tenant
  [ ] Display name and description make its purpose obvious (svc-pa-finance, "Finance flows")
  [ ] No mailbox rules, forwarding or personal use
  Credentials
  [ ] Password stored in a vault, not a document or chat
  [ ] Everyone who knows it is listed and still needs it. Rotated since the last leaver.
  [ ] MFA enforced. If excluded, a Conditional Access policy restricts sign-in by location or device.
  [ ] Sign-in logs (Entra > Sign-in logs, filter by the UPN) show only expected apps and locations
  Licences and limits
  [ ] Has the licence its flows need (premium connectors need Power Automate Premium, or flows on a Process plan)
  [ ] Request usage is within limits: one account running many flows shares one daily allowance
  Access
  [ ] No Global Admin, Power Platform Admin or SharePoint Admin role unless documented and needed
  [ ] Site access is at the lowest level that works (Edit on specific sites, not site collection admin)
  [ ] Dataverse security role is a specific role, not System Administrator
  [ ] Shared mailbox permissions are limited to the mailboxes it sends from
  Flows and connections
  [ ] Every flow it owns has a human co-owner
  [ ] No connections with errors or "Fix connection" status
  [ ] Connections not used by any flow are deleted
  [ ] Flows turned off for more than 90 days are reviewed for deletion

Gather the facts (PowerShell)
  Add-PowerAppsAccount
  $upn = "svc-pa-finance@contoso.com"
  $id  = (Get-AzureADUser -ObjectId $upn).ObjectId        # or Get-MgUser -UserId $upn
  Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment | ForEach-Object {
      $envName = $_.EnvironmentName; $envDisplay = $_.DisplayName
      Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $envName | Where-Object { $_.CreatedBy.objectId -eq $id } |
        Select-Object @{n="Environment";e={$envDisplay}}, DisplayName, Enabled, LastModifiedTime
  } | Export-Csv svc-flows.csv -NoTypeInformation
  Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment | ForEach-Object {
      Get-AdminPowerAppConnection -EnvironmentName $_.EnvironmentName | Where-Object { $_.CreatedBy.id -eq $id } |
        Select-Object ConnectorName, DisplayName, @{n="Status";e={$_.Statuses.status}}
  } | Export-Csv svc-connections.csv -NoTypeInformation
  Directory roles: Entra admin centre > Users > the account > Assigned roles.
  Licences:        Microsoft 365 admin centre > Users > the account > Licences and apps.

Decide
  Keep as is            All checks pass. Set NextReview + 6 months.
  Keep with actions     List actions with owners and dates: rotate password, remove role, add co-owners.
  Split                 One account spanning unrelated areas becomes one per area, so a compromise or lockout
                        affects less.
  Replace               Dataverse and custom-connector flows can run under a service principal (application
                        user) with no password or licence-per-user sign-in. Standard connectors such as
                        SharePoint and Outlook still need a user connection.
  Retire                No enabled flows. Disable sign-in, wait 30 days, delete.

Rotation without an outage
  Change the password, then open Connections signed in as the account and fix any that show an error.
  Run one flow per connector as a test. Record the date and who now holds the credential.

Report: accounts reviewed, excluded from MFA, with admin roles, with no business owner, actions open past due.
stepByStepInstructions: List every service account that owns flows or connections in a register with owners and purpose.
Export the flows and connections each account holds.
Work through the identity, credential, licence, access and flow checks.
Review sign-in logs for unexpected use.
Decide to keep, fix, split, replace with a service principal or retire, and assign actions.
Rotate credentials where needed, retest flows and set the next review date.
commonMistakes: One service account for the whole tenant.
Excluding the account from MFA with no compensating policy.
Granting admin roles to make connector errors go away.
Credentials known by people who have left.
troubleshooting: If flows fail after a password change, reauthenticate each connection signed in as the service account.
If flows are throttled, too many share one account's request allowance. Split the account or assign Process licences.
If premium actions fail, the account lacks a premium licence or the flow is not covered by a per-flow plan.
If MFA prompts break connections, use a phishing-resistant method on a controlled device and a Conditional Access policy scoped to the account.

faqs.question: How often should Power Automate service accounts be reviewed?
faqs.answer: At least every six months, and whenever someone who knows the credentials leaves.

faqs.question: Should service accounts have MFA?
faqs.answer: Yes. If an account is excluded, restrict it with Conditional Access and monitor its sign-ins.

faqs.question: Can a service principal replace a service account for flows?
faqs.answer: For Dataverse and some connectors, yes. Connectors such as SharePoint and Outlook still need a user account.

create-a-run-history-review-cadence.shortDescription: A fixed weekly and monthly routine for reviewing flow run history across production flows, so failures, slow runs and silent problems are found by the team, not by users.
create-a-run-history-review-cadence.fullDescription: Run history is kept for 28 days and nobody looks at it until something is reported. A review cadence makes it a habit: a short weekly check of failures and durations for each production flow, a monthly look at trends, and a clear rule for what gets logged or fixed. Automated collection does the counting so the meeting is about decisions.
create-a-run-history-review-cadence.problemStatement: A nightly sync has been failing one run in five for two months. Each failure sent an email to an owner who filters them to a folder, and the gap in the data is found at quarter end.
whenToUse: Teams supporting ten or more production flows
Flows where a missed run has business impact
Environments without a monitoring tool already in place
whenNotToUse: Responding to a single failed run, which is triage
Tenants with the CoE Starter Kit or Azure Monitor dashboards already reviewed on a schedule
create-a-run-history-review-cadence.formulaOrCode:
Scope: the production flow list (from the flow inventory), each with an expected pattern:
  Flow                    Trigger        Expected runs      Normal duration   Criticality   Owner
  Invoice approval        Item created   20 to 60 a day     under 2 min*      High          A. Khan
  Nightly finance sync    Recurrence     1 a day at 02:00   8 to 15 min       High          Service acct
  Weekly digest           Recurrence     1 a week           under 1 min       Low           J. Lee
  * excluding time spent waiting on approvals

Weekly review (30 minutes, same day each week, rota of two people)
  For each flow, in criticality order:
  1. Failed runs in the last 7 days: count and group by failed action.
        Portal: flow > 28-day run history > All runs > filter Failed.
        Cloud flow activity: make.powerautomate.com > More > Cloud flow activity (failures across flows).
  2. Did it run when expected? Zero runs for a scheduled flow is a failure that sends no alert.
        Check the flow is On and the last run time matches the schedule.
  3. Duration outliers: runs taking more than twice the normal duration.
  4. Cancelled and long-running runs: approvals or waits still open after 14 days (runs time out at 30 days).
  5. Throttling and retries: open one typical run and look for actions with retries or 429 responses.
  6. Skipped runs caused by trigger conditions: confirm the count looks plausible.
  Record per flow: runs, failed, failure rate, longest run, action needed (yes/no).

Thresholds (agree once)
  Failure rate over 2% for High, 5% for others            -> incident entry in the support log
  Same action failing in two consecutive weeks            -> permanent fix scheduled
  Scheduled flow missed a run                             -> same-day investigation
  Duration doubled over four weeks                        -> performance review of the flow
  Flow suspended or turned off by the platform            -> same-day fix (flows failing continuously are
                                                             turned off after 14 days)

Collect the numbers automatically (scheduled flow, weekly, Power Automate Management connector)
  List Flows as Admin (or a fixed array of flow IDs from the inventory)
  For each flow:
    HTTP with Microsoft Entra ID (preauthorized) or the Flow management API:
      GET https://api.flow.microsoft.com/providers/Microsoft.ProcessSimple/environments/{env}/flows/{flowId}/runs
          ?api-version=2016-11-01&$filter=startTime ge @{addDays(utcNow(),-7)}&$top=250
    Select: status, startTime, endTime
    Compose: total = length(value)
             failed = length(Filter array where status eq 'Failed')
             maxMinutes = max duration from div(sub(ticks(endTime),ticks(startTime)),600000000)
    Create item in "Run History Weekly": Flow, WeekStarting, Runs, Failed, FailureRate, MaxMinutes
  Dataverse alternative: solution-aware flows write runs to the FlowRun table (flowruns), which can be
  filtered with List rows and kept longer than 28 days by adjusting the retention setting.

Review list views
  This week, action needed     FailureRate over threshold OR Runs = 0
  Trend by flow                Grouped by Flow, last 12 weeks
  Missed schedules             Runs = 0 for flows with a Recurrence trigger

Monthly review (45 minutes, with flow owners)
  Trend of failure rate per flow over 12 weeks.     Top five failing actions across all flows.
  Flows approaching limits: runs per day, actions per run, API requests per account.
  Connections expiring or owned by leavers.          Flows with no runs in 60 days: still needed?
  Open follow-ups from the support log.              One improvement picked and assigned.

Roles
  Reviewer (rota): runs the weekly check, raises entries.   Flow owner: fixes within the agreed time.
  Service owner: chairs the monthly review, signs off the report.

Evidence kept: the weekly list rows, support log entries and a one-page monthly summary.
stepByStepInstructions: List production flows with expected run counts, normal duration, criticality and owner.
Agree thresholds for failure rate, missed runs and duration that trigger action.
Run a 30-minute weekly review of failures, missed schedules, slow and stuck runs.
Automate collection of weekly run counts and failures into a list.
Hold a monthly review of trends, limits, unused flows and open follow-ups.
Record findings in the support log and assign fixes with dates.
commonMistakes: Looking at run history only after a complaint.
Checking failures but not flows that did not run at all.
Reviewing without thresholds, so nothing leads to action.
Relying on failure emails sent to one owner.
troubleshooting: If history is gone, runs are kept for 28 days. Log weekly counts to a list to keep trends.
If a scheduled flow shows no runs, check whether it was turned off after repeated failures.
If the management API call fails, check the connection's account has access to the environment and flow.
If the review overruns, cover high-criticality flows weekly and the rest fortnightly.

faqs.question: How long does Power Automate keep run history?
faqs.answer: 28 days for cloud flows. Keep your own weekly counts or use Dataverse flow run records to see longer trends.

faqs.question: How often should flow run history be reviewed?
faqs.answer: Weekly for failures, missed schedules and slow runs, with a monthly review of trends and limits.

faqs.question: How do I spot a scheduled flow that stopped running?
faqs.answer: Compare the number of runs with the expected schedule. Zero runs sends no failure alert, so it must be checked.

create-a-flow-environment-inventory.shortDescription: An inventory of every cloud flow in each environment with owner, state, trigger, connectors and last run, built by script or flow, to answer what runs where and who is responsible.
create-a-flow-environment-inventory.fullDescription: Before you can govern, license or migrate flows you need to know what exists. A flow environment inventory lists every flow per environment with the facts that drive decisions: who owns it, whether it is on, what triggers it, which connectors it uses, whether it sits in a solution and when it last ran. It is refreshed on a schedule and reviewed for exceptions.
create-a-flow-environment-inventory.problemStatement: An admin is asked how many flows use the SQL connector in production and who owns them. The answer takes a week of clicking through the admin centre, and is out of date when delivered.
whenToUse: Tenant or environment admins preparing for licensing, DLP or migration work
Environment owners accountable for what runs in their environment
A lighter alternative when the CoE Starter Kit is not installed
whenNotToUse: Documenting how one team's flows work, which is a documentation template per flow
Tenants already running the CoE Starter Kit inventory, which collects the same data
create-a-flow-environment-inventory.formulaOrCode:
Target list (or Dataverse table): Flow Inventory
  Title (flow display name), FlowId (text, indexed, unique), EnvironmentName, EnvironmentId,
  EnvironmentType (Default, Production, Sandbox, Developer), State (Started, Stopped, Suspended),
  OwnerName, OwnerEmail, OwnerActive (yes/no), CoOwners (text), TriggerType (text), Connectors (text),
  PremiumConnectors (yes/no), InSolution (yes/no), CreatedOn, ModifiedOn, LastRun (date), LastRunStatus,
  BusinessOwner (person, filled by review), Criticality (choice, filled by review), LastSeen (date), Notes

Collect with PowerShell (admin; Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell)
  Add-PowerAppsAccount
  $rows = foreach ($env in Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment) {
    foreach ($f in Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName) {
      $detail = Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName $env.EnvironmentName -FlowName $f.FlowName
      $refs   = $detail.Internal.properties.connectionReferences
      $conns  = if ($refs) { ($refs.PSObject.Properties.Value | ForEach-Object { $_.displayName }) | Sort-Object -Unique } else { @() }
      [pscustomobject]@{
        Flow            = $f.DisplayName
        FlowId          = $f.FlowName
        Environment     = $env.DisplayName
        EnvironmentId   = $env.EnvironmentName
        EnvironmentType = $env.EnvironmentType
        State           = $detail.Internal.properties.state
        OwnerId         = $f.CreatedBy.objectId
        TriggerType     = ($detail.Internal.properties.definitionSummary.triggers | Select-Object -First 1).type
        Connectors      = $conns -join "; "
        Created         = $f.CreatedTime
        Modified        = $f.LastModifiedTime
      }
    }
  }
  $rows | Export-Csv flow-inventory.csv -NoTypeInformation
  Resolve owners:  Get-MgUser -UserId <OwnerId> -Property DisplayName, Mail, AccountEnabled
  An error or AccountEnabled false means the flow is orphaned.

Collect with a flow (no admin PowerShell needed, scheduled weekly)
  Power Platform for Admins: List Environments as Admin
  For each environment -> Power Automate Management: List Flows as Admin (V2)
    For each flow -> Get Flow as Admin (connection references, state, definition summary)
       SharePoint Get items where FlowId eq the flow name
         found     -> Update item (State, ModifiedOn, Connectors, LastSeen = today)
         not found -> Create item
  After the loops: Get items where LastSeen lt today -> mark State "Deleted" (do not delete rows; history matters).
  Concurrency on the inner loop: 10 to 20. Expect minutes per thousand flows.

Enrich
  Premium connectors: compare Connectors with a list of premium connector names (SQL Server, HTTP,
     Dataverse outside Dynamics, Azure services, custom connectors). Set PremiumConnectors.
  InSolution: solution-aware flows appear in the Dataverse workflows table (category 5):
     List rows: workflows, filter category eq 5, select name, workflowidunique, statecode, _ownerid_value
  Last run: Dataverse flowruns for solution flows, or the management API runs endpoint with $top=1.

Views
  By environment            Grouped by EnvironmentName, Count
  Orphaned                  OwnerActive = No AND State = Started
  Default environment, on   EnvironmentType = Default AND State = Started
  Premium connector use     PremiumConnectors = Yes, grouped by OwnerName
  Suspended or stopped      State <> Started, sorted by ModifiedOn
  Not in a solution (prod)  EnvironmentType = Production AND InSolution = No
  No business owner         BusinessOwner is blank AND EnvironmentType = Production

Review each month
  Orphaned flows reassigned or turned off.          Production flows outside solutions scheduled for move.
  Premium use matched against licences.              Stopped flows older than 90 days confirmed for deletion.
  New flows in production environments checked for a business owner and criticality.

Questions the inventory answers in one filter
  Which flows use connector X? Who owns flows in environment Y? What breaks when user Z leaves?
  How many flows does a DLP policy change affect?
stepByStepInstructions: Create the inventory list or table with flow, environment, owner, state, trigger and connector columns.
Collect flows per environment with the admin PowerShell module or the admin connectors.
Resolve owners against the directory and flag disabled or missing accounts.
Enrich with premium connector use, solution membership and last run.
Upsert weekly, marking flows no longer seen as deleted.
Review exception views monthly and fill in business owner and criticality.
commonMistakes: A one-off spreadsheet that is never refreshed.
Listing flows without their connectors.
Deleting inventory rows when a flow disappears.
Collecting data and never reviewing the exceptions.
troubleshooting: If the script returns only your own flows, sign in with a Power Platform admin account and use the admin cmdlets.
If connectors are blank, read connection references from the flow detail call, not the list call.
If the collecting flow times out, process one environment per run or raise loop concurrency.
If owners show as IDs, resolve them with Microsoft Graph and store the name and email.

faqs.question: How do I list all flows in a Power Platform environment?
faqs.answer: Use Get-AdminFlow in the admin PowerShell module, or List Flows as Admin in the Power Automate Management connector.

faqs.question: How do I find which flows use a specific connector?
faqs.answer: Read each flow's connection references into the inventory, then filter on the connector name.

faqs.question: How do I find flows with no owner?
faqs.answer: Resolve each flow's creator against the directory and flag accounts that are disabled or no longer exist.

create-a-production-flow-support-model.shortDescription: A tiered support model for production flows: criticality classes, response targets, who handles what at each tier, and the alerting and runbooks that make it work.
create-a-production-flow-support-model.fullDescription: Not every flow deserves the same support. A model that classes flows by business impact and sets a response target for each lets a small team give a payroll flow real cover without promising the same for a weekly reminder. It defines the tiers of people involved, what each can do, how failures reach them and what must exist before a flow is accepted into support.
create-a-production-flow-support-model.problemStatement: Every flow failure goes to the maker who built it. Critical flows fail at night with no cover, trivial ones generate the same noise, and the business has no stated expectation of how quickly anything is fixed.
whenToUse: Organisations with business-critical flows built by makers
IT or platform teams taking flows into formal support
Agreeing expectations with business owners
whenNotToUse: Naming the individual owners of each flow, which is the ownership model
A handful of personal productivity flows
create-a-production-flow-support-model.formulaOrCode:
1. Criticality classes
   Class   Meaning                                   Examples                         Respond   Restore    Hours
   A       Stops a core process or has legal,        Payroll file, order intake,      30 min    4 hours    Business hours + on-call
           financial or safety impact                 regulatory notice
   B       Degrades a team's work; manual            Approvals, onboarding tasks,     4 hours   2 days     Business hours
           workaround exists                          sync to reporting
   C       Convenience                                Digests, reminders, tidy-up      2 days    Best effort Business hours
   Class is set by the business owner with the platform team, recorded in the flow inventory.

2. Tiers
   Tier 0  Self-healing: retry policies, error handling scopes, idempotent design, automatic resubmit where safe.
   Tier 1  Service desk or operations: sees the alert, checks the runbook, resubmits a failed run, turns a
           flow on, fixes an expired connection (if trained), informs users. Does not edit flows.
   Tier 2  Flow owner or maker team: diagnoses, edits logic, fixes data, deploys through the pipeline.
   Tier 3  Platform team: environment, DLP, licensing, capacity, connector and service issues, Microsoft support tickets.
   Business owner: decides on workarounds, priorities and communication to users.

3. What each class must have before it is accepted into support
   Requirement                                    A          B          C
   In a managed solution in production            Required   Required   Recommended
   Owned by a service account or principal,       Required   Required   Recommended
     with two human co-owners
   Try/Catch scope with failure alert             Required   Required   Recommended
   Alert destination                              On-call    Team       Owner
                                                  channel    channel    email
   Run logging to a list or table                 Required   Recommended  No
   Runbook (symptoms, checks, safe actions)       Required   Required   No
   Tested rollback (previous solution version)    Required   Recommended  No
   Monitoring for "did not run"                   Required   Recommended  No
   Business owner and criticality in inventory    Required   Required   Required
   Reviewed in weekly run history check           Weekly     Weekly     Monthly

4. Alert routing
   Catch scope -> child flow "Raise flow alert" with { flowName, environment, class, failedAction, error, runUrl }
     Class A -> adaptive card to the On-call channel with a mention, and a ticket in the service desk tool
     Class B -> post to the team's support channel, entry in the support log
     Class C -> email to the owner, daily digest of failures
   Scheduled heartbeat check (every 30 min) for Class A recurrence flows: no successful run inside the
   expected window raises the same alert.

5. Runbook template (one page per flow)
   Purpose and business owner | Trigger and schedule | What a failure looks like to users
   Common failures:  symptom -> check -> safe action for Tier 1 -> when to escalate
   Safe to resubmit? (yes / only after checking for a partial write / never)
   Manual workaround while the flow is down | Contacts for Tier 2 and Tier 3 | Last tested date

6. Escalation path and clock
   Alert received -> Tier 1 acknowledges within the Respond target.
   Not resolved with the runbook in 30 minutes (A) or 4 hours (B) -> Tier 2.
   Platform or service cause suspected -> Tier 3 at once, and check the Microsoft 365 service health page.
   Class A past half its Restore target -> service owner and business owner informed, workaround started.

7. Change control by class
   A: tested in a test environment, deployed by pipeline with approval, outside business peaks.
   B: tested, deployed by pipeline.          C: owner may deploy directly, still from a solution.
   No editing of production flows in place for A and B except a documented emergency fix, back-ported the same day.

8. Measures (monthly)
   Incidents by class, response and restore times against target, repeat incidents, flows accepted this month,
   flows running in production outside the model.

9. Onboarding a flow into support
   Request -> class agreed -> checklist in section 3 completed -> walkthrough with Tier 1 -> inventory updated -> accepted.
   A flow that fails the checklist stays the maker's responsibility until it passes.
stepByStepInstructions: Define criticality classes with response and restore targets and get business agreement.
Define the support tiers and what each is allowed to do.
Set the acceptance requirements each class must meet before entering support.
Route failure alerts by class through one shared alert flow and add a did-not-run check for critical flows.
Write a one-page runbook for each class A and B flow.
Set escalation timings, change rules by class and report monthly against the targets.
commonMistakes: The same promise for every flow.
Tier 1 expected to act with no runbook.
Critical flows accepted into support while owned by a personal account.
Alerts sent by email to one maker.
troubleshooting: If everything is classed A, require the business owner to state the cost of a day's outage and reclassify.
If Tier 1 escalates everything, improve the runbooks' safe actions and train on resubmit and connection repair.
If alerts are missed out of hours, route class A to the on-call tool as well as Teams.
If makers bypass the model, block production deployments outside the pipeline for class A and B.

faqs.question: How should production Power Automate flows be supported?
faqs.answer: Class flows by business impact, set response targets per class, and define tiers from self-healing through service desk, owner and platform team.

faqs.question: What should a flow have before IT supports it?
faqs.answer: A solution deployment, non-personal ownership with co-owners, error handling with alerts, a runbook, a named business owner and a criticality class.

faqs.question: Who can resubmit a failed flow run?
faqs.answer: Tier 1 support can, when the runbook says a resubmit is safe for that flow.

create-an-environment-strategy-guide.shortDescription: A short written guide that tells makers and admins which environment to use for what, how to get one, the naming and security rules, and when an environment is retired.
create-an-environment-strategy-guide.fullDescription: An environment strategy only works when people can read it. The guide turns the strategy into a few pages: the environment types on offer, a decision table for where a piece of work belongs, how to request an environment, the naming convention, who gets which role, the DLP policy that applies and the lifecycle rules. It is the document linked from the welcome email and the request form.
create-an-environment-strategy-guide.problemStatement: Admins have agreed an environment structure, but it lives in a slide deck. Makers still build in the default environment and ask in chat where things should go, and every answer is slightly different.
whenToUse: After an environment strategy has been agreed and needs to be published
Tenants with more than a handful of environments or makers
Onboarding new makers and project teams
whenNotToUse: Deciding the strategy itself, which comes first
Tenants with a single team and three fixed environments, where a one-paragraph note is enough
create-an-environment-strategy-guide.formulaOrCode:
ENVIRONMENT STRATEGY GUIDE            Version 1.3   Owner: Platform team   Reviewed: every 6 months

1. Environments we offer
   Type            Purpose                                  Who can create    Dataverse   Managed   Backups
